title: System Design · Interview Lab
description: 60 interview lessons across 20 case studies. Import this standalone course to begin the interview track immediately.

lessons.title: Short links: frame the design
lessons.summary: URL shortener · Part 1 of 3: requirements & api.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a service that turns long URLs into short links.
Ask whether links expire, support custom aliases, or collect analytics.
Assume public links and 10 million new links per day for this exercise.
Start with creation and redirection; postpone analytics until the core works.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Creation and redirection have very different traffic patterns.
A mapping must survive restarts; a cache alone is insufficient.
Custom aliases create a uniqueness requirement under concurrent requests.
Decide whether destinations are immutable before choosing redirect caching.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Expose POST /links with a destination and optional expiration.
Return a code; GET /{code} looks up the stored destination.
Store code, destination, owner, created_at, and expires_at.
Enforce uniqueness on code and reject unsupported destination schemes.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The create handler validates input and inserts one mapping.
The redirect handler looks up the code and checks expiration.
It returns a redirect whose caching policy matches product semantics.
A missing or expired link returns a deliberate error, not an arbitrary URL.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d clarify custom aliases and expiration before drawing components.”
“My baseline is an API plus a durable, indexed mapping store.”
“The redirect endpoint is the critical latency path.”
“I’d add caching only after estimating its traffic and freshness needs.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why not hash the destination and stop there?
A shortened hash can collide, and different owners may need different policies.
Random codes plus a unique constraint are a simple alternative.
If insertion collides, generate another code and retry within a bound.

quiz.question: Two users claim the same alias simultaneously. What protects ownership?
options: A unique constraint on the alias
A prior read without a constraint
quiz.explanation: Both reads can see an absent alias. Atomic uniqueness makes only one insert succeed.

quiz.question: Which requirement changes redirect caching decisions?
quiz.explanation: A cached redirect may bypass your service, making destination changes slow to reach clients.

quiz.question: What belongs on the redirect critical path?
options: A full scan of all links
quiz.explanation: The redirect needs the destination and its validity; analytics should not delay navigation.

lessons.title: Short links: size the read path
lessons.summary: URL shortener · Part 2 of 3: capacity & caching.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The interviewer adds: redirects outnumber creates by 100 to one.
At 10 million creates daily, assume one billion redirects daily.
That averages about 11,600 redirects per second over 86,400 seconds.
Use a separate peak assumption; averages do not size a launch-day spike.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Suppose each mapping occupies 500 bytes before storage overhead.
Ten million mappings add roughly 5 GB of raw data per day.
Indexes, replicas, metadata, and backups multiply the real storage need.
Retention determines whether this growth continues indefinitely.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Cache popular code-to-destination mappings with bounded expiration.
On a miss, read the authoritative store and populate the cache.
Choose TTL from tolerated staleness, not a round number alone.
Coalesce simultaneous misses so one popular link does not overload storage.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A redirect first checks the cache using the short code.
A hit supplies the destination, but the handler still enforces expiry.
A miss uses the indexed database lookup and fills the cache.
Asynchronous analytics receive an event outside the response path.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I estimate reads, writes, and storage separately.”
“With a hypothetical 95% cache hit rate, average source reads are about 580 per second.”
“That estimate excludes writes, peaks, and cache-loss traffic.”
“I would size a degraded path rather than assume the cache always works.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if the cache disappears during peak traffic?
Blindly forwarding every miss can collapse the database.
Bound concurrency, shed excess load, and protect the source capacity.
Warm important keys gradually; restoration itself can create a traffic spike.

quiz.question: At one billion redirects daily, which average rate is closest?
quiz.explanation: Divide the daily count by 86,400; then separately model the peak multiplier.

quiz.question: Does a 95% hit rate prove the database survives cache loss?
options: Yes; the database load stays constant
quiz.explanation: With the cache unavailable, the source may face nearly the full read load unless protected.

quiz.question: Why is 5 GB per day only a starting estimate?
options: It excludes indexes, replicas, and other overhead
It already includes every backup forever
quiz.explanation: Raw record size estimates must be expanded for the chosen storage system and retention policy.

lessons.title: Short links: hot keys & safe changes
lessons.summary: URL shortener · Part 3 of 3: failure & consistency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A celebrity shares one link, then its owner disables it.
The interviewer asks how quickly that disable takes effect.
A high cache hit rate helps load but can hide a recent change.
Clarify whether revocation is best-effort or has a strict deadline.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
One hot code concentrates requests even across many database shards.
Adding shards does not split repeated reads for that single key.
Cached redirects in clients or CDNs may bypass your own API entirely.
Any promised revocation deadline must account for those caches too.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
For mutable links, avoid long-lived permanent redirect caching.
Invalidate service caches after writes and bound remaining staleness with TTL.
Use versioned values or ordered updates to reduce stale cache repopulation.
For strict revocation, enforce an authoritative check or a carefully bounded deny path.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
An owner update commits the disabled state in durable storage.
An outbox event requests cache invalidation after that commit.
Consumers retry invalidation; expiration limits missed invalidations.
If the product requires instant revocation, this asynchronous path alone is insufficient.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would ask how quickly a disabled link must stop working.”
“For a bounded-delay policy, I combine invalidation with short TTLs.”
“I would not promise instant revocation through a long-cached redirect.”
“The stronger guarantee costs additional coordination or origin checks.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why use an outbox rather than publish after the write?
The process can crash between committing the row and publishing an event.
An outbox stores the event intent in the same database transaction.
A relay may publish twice, so invalidation consumers must tolerate duplicates.

quiz.question: Why might database sharding fail to solve a viral link spike?
options: Every shard must accept the same write
One key still receives most requests
quiz.explanation: Skewed traffic remains concentrated on the partition owning that key; caching or replication can help reads.

quiz.question: What does an outbox address?
options: The gap between committing data and publishing an event
quiz.explanation: The event intent is committed atomically with the data, then relayed with retry and deduplication.

quiz.question: Which claim is unsafe with long-lived cached redirects?
quiz.explanation: A client may keep following a cached redirect without consulting the service.

lessons.title: Rate limits: define fairness first
lessons.summary: API rate limiter · Part 1 of 3: requirements & algorithm.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a shared rate limiter for a public inference API.
Ask whether limits apply per user, tenant, IP, or model.
Assume each tenant gets 100 requests per second with a burst of 200.
Those are practice values; a real limit should reflect cost and capacity.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A fixed window counter is easy to implement but has a boundary burst.
A caller can spend one window’s allowance just before its end.
It can spend the next allowance immediately after the boundary.
Decide whether that behavior is acceptable before choosing the algorithm.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
A token bucket refills tokens at a configured rate up to capacity.
Each accepted request consumes tokens; an empty bucket rejects or delays.
A capacity of 200 permits short bursts while refill limits sustained use.
For variable-cost inference, charge estimated cost rather than counting every request equally.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Authenticate the request before applying its tenant-specific allowance.
Check and consume tokens atomically using the bucket identity.
Accepted requests reach the model service; rejected requests receive 429.
Include retry guidance when a meaningful next-eligible time can be calculated.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d define the identity and the resource we are protecting first.”
“A token bucket fits bounded bursts with a steady refill rate.”
“I would use weighted tokens if model requests have different costs.”
“My response contract includes 429 and clear retry behavior.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does this stop every overload scenario?
No; a tenant rate limit is different from a global concurrency limit.
Long-running requests can exhaust workers even at a modest request rate.
Combine rate limits with admission control for the expensive execution stage.

quiz.question: Why choose a token bucket here?
options: It supports bounded bursts and steady refill
It makes all model requests equally expensive
quiz.explanation: Bucket capacity controls burst allowance; the refill rate controls long-run spending.

quiz.question: Why can a fixed window allow a boundary spike?
options: It automatically rejects every second request
Adjacent windows each have their own allowance
quiz.explanation: Calls near opposite sides of a boundary can consume two allowances in a very short interval.

quiz.question: What protects workers from many slow requests?
options: A concurrency limit in addition to rate limits
A larger font on the error page
quiz.explanation: In-flight work consumes resources for its entire duration, so request rate alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: Rate limits: make the decision atomic
lessons.summary: API rate limiter · Part 2 of 3: distributed coordination.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The API now runs on twenty workers behind a load balancer.
Each worker must enforce the same tenant allowance.
A separate in-memory bucket per worker multiplies the effective limit.
The interviewer wants a shared decision without excessive network latency.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Reading a balance and writing it back are two separate operations.
Concurrent workers may all observe the same available token.
Each can approve a request before any updated balance is visible.
The resulting race violates the limit even if every individual read is correct.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Keep bucket state in Redis and combine refill, check, and consume atomically.
A short server-side script can execute this update for one bucket.
Store token balance and last-refill time; expire long-idle buckets safely.
Use a consistent time source and clamp negative elapsed time defensively.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A worker sends the bucket key, policy, and request cost.
The atomic operation calculates refill and returns allow or deny.
All state required for that decision belongs to the same atomic scope.
With clustered Redis, avoid a script spanning unrelated hash slots.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would not implement this as a separate GET and SET.”
“The refill calculation and token debit must happen atomically.”
“I’d keep the script short and one bucket’s state together.”
“Then I’d measure the extra round-trip latency and hot-tenant load.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if one tenant’s bucket becomes a hot key?
That shared key can bottleneck even a large Redis cluster.
Local token leases can reduce calls but require careful allowance accounting.
I’d introduce that complexity only if measured traffic justifies it.

quiz.question: Why is separate GET then SET unsafe?
options: Workers can consume the same observed allowance
quiz.explanation: Read-modify-write must be coordinated to prevent concurrent overspending.

quiz.question: What should the atomic operation include?
quiz.explanation: Splitting any of the decision’s shared-state steps can reintroduce a race.

quiz.question: Why might clustered Redis constrain the key layout?
options: Multi-key atomic work must fit supported slot rules
Every key must share one global password
quiz.explanation: Keep the relevant state together so the chosen atomic primitive is actually supported.

lessons.title: Rate limits: outages and regional budgets
lessons.summary: API rate limiter · Part 3 of 3: degraded operation.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The limiter’s Redis cluster is unreachable for several seconds.
Should the API accept requests or reject them?
Ask what an outage costs: lost availability, abuse, money, or resource exhaustion.
There is no universally correct fail-open policy for every endpoint.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Fail-open keeps the service accessible but loses strict shared enforcement.
Fail-closed protects the resource but turns a limiter outage into an API outage.
An unbounded fallback can overwhelm expensive inference workers.
A per-process fallback is approximate and changes when replicas scale.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a bounded local fallback when the product permits approximate limits.
Protect global expensive work with a separate concurrency budget.
For regions, allocate regional budgets whose sum fits the global allowance.
Independent full-size buckets in every region silently multiply the global limit.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Normal requests consult the shared limiter with a short timeout.
On failure, a documented policy chooses rejection or conservative local admission.
Metrics record both degraded mode and the estimated enforcement error.
Recovery avoids resetting every tenant to a fresh, full burst without thought.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d choose outage behavior per endpoint, based on the cost of excess work.”
“For paid inference I would prefer bounded degradation over unlimited admission.”
“A strict global quota needs coordination or explicitly allocated budgets.”
“I would state the availability cost of that stronger guarantee.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can regional budgets waste capacity?
Yes; one region may run out while another has unused tokens.
Rebalancing improves utilization but requires safe ownership and accounting.
The tradeoff is coordination overhead versus predictable global enforcement.

quiz.question: What is wrong with a full global allowance in every region?
options: Total permitted traffic can multiply by region count
It automatically enforces a stricter global limit
quiz.explanation: Independent full budgets are not one shared global budget.

quiz.question: Which fallback best bounds expensive inference work?
options: Conservative local admission plus concurrency limits
quiz.explanation: A bounded fallback reduces availability damage while still protecting finite execution resources.

quiz.question: What is a cost of fixed regional budget allocation?
options: No region can ever serve traffic
Unused allowance can be stranded in another region
quiz.explanation: Capacity partitioning preserves bounds but can reduce utilization when demand is uneven.

lessons.title: Product cache: choose what may be stale
lessons.summary: Product cache · Part 1 of 3: access patterns & freshness.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design caching for a product detail page during a sale.
The page contains a description, price, inventory, and recommendations.
Ask which fields can tolerate seconds or minutes of staleness.
Treat checkout correctness separately from the speed of browsing.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A single cached page mixes fields with different freshness needs.
Descriptions rarely change, while stock can change on every order.
Displaying cached stock as a promise can cause overselling.
Caching strategy should follow business guarantees, not just endpoint boundaries.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Cache stable product details with a longer TTL.
Give volatile display fields shorter lifetimes or fetch them separately.
At checkout, validate price policy and reserve stock against authoritative state.
Include product version or locale in keys when the response depends on them.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A page request loads reusable details from a cache.
It adds freshness-sensitive information under a separate policy.
The customer submits an order referencing the displayed offer or version.
Checkout performs the authoritative eligibility and inventory checks.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d split browsing freshness from purchase correctness.”
“A cached stock count is a hint, not a reservation.”
“The cache key must include every input that changes the result.”
“I would revalidate the critical purchase rules in the write path.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can every product share one cache key shape?
Only if all response-affecting dimensions are represented correctly.
Tenant, locale, permissions, and currency can change the response.
Omitting authorization scope can leak one customer’s data to another.

quiz.question: Can cached availability guarantee a successful purchase?
options: No; stock must be reserved authoritatively
Yes if the TTL is under one minute
quiz.explanation: A different customer can consume stock between viewing and purchase.

quiz.question: Which dimension may need to be in a cache key?
quiz.explanation: Reusing results across authorization contexts can expose data incorrectly.

quiz.question: Why split cached descriptions from stock?
quiz.explanation: Separate policies avoid imposing one field’s freshness or cost requirements on every field.

lessons.title: Product cache: survive a cold start
lessons.summary: Product cache · Part 2 of 3: stampedes & capacity.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A popular sale page expires while thousands of customers arrive.
Every request misses the same key at nearly the same moment.
The database becomes the unexpected bottleneck.
Explain how to reduce duplicate work without making correctness depend on a lock.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A cache miss does not imply that nobody else is fetching the value.
Uncoordinated workers all repeat the same expensive query.
A distributed lock can help, but leases expire and holders can crash.
A lock should optimize fetch work, not become the only source of truth.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Coalesce in-flight fetches for the same key within each process.
For large cross-process spikes, use a short fetch lease where appropriate.
Allow stale-while-revalidate only for fields whose staleness is acceptable.
Add TTL jitter across different keys to spread synchronized expiration.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
One worker becomes the refresher and fetches the source.
Other requests receive allowed stale data or wait within a bound.
The refresher updates the cache and releases its lease when possible.
Failures fall back to bounded source access rather than unbounded waiting.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would first avoid duplicated in-flight work for each hot key.”
“I’d serve stale descriptions during refresh if the product permits it.”
“TTL jitter spreads many keys, but does not solve one hot key alone.”
“I would bound refresh time and database concurrency.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does cache warming solve all cold-start problems?
Warming every key can overload the source before real users arrive.
Prioritize a measured hot set and rate-limit the warm-up workload.
A system still needs a safe miss path for uncached or new products.

quiz.question: What directly reduces duplicate fetches for one hot key?
quiz.explanation: Coalescing shares one in-flight fetch among callers instead of repeating the same work.

quiz.question: What does TTL jitter primarily spread?
quiz.explanation: Jitter avoids a large set of keys expiring together; a single hot key still needs its own strategy.

quiz.question: When is stale-while-revalidate appropriate?
options: When that field can tolerate the bounded staleness
Only when the database is empty
quiz.explanation: Serving stale values is a product-level freshness decision, not a universal optimization.

lessons.title: Product cache: explain the invalidation race
lessons.summary: Product cache · Part 3 of 3: versioning & failure.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A product description is updated, yet the old text returns to the cache.
The writer successfully deleted the cache entry after its database commit.
The interviewer asks how this can still happen.
Walk through concurrent operations instead of claiming deletion solves everything.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Reader A misses the cache and reads the old database value.
Writer B commits a new value and invalidates the cache.
Reader A finishes later and stores the old value it fetched earlier.
The cache is stale again even though invalidation succeeded.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use version-aware writes or a coordinated refresh path when needed.
An older value must not replace a newer known version.
Keep a TTL as a recovery bound for missed events or stale fills.
Stronger freshness can require bypassing the cache for specific reads.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A write stores the updated record and its monotonic version.
An outbox event carries the affected key and new version.
Cache consumers reject older updates under an atomic version check.
Do not discard all version knowledge and assume stale fills become impossible.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d demonstrate the stale-fill race before proposing a fix.”
“Deleting after a write reduces staleness but does not guarantee its absence.”
“For stricter reads, I’d compare versions or read the authoritative store.”
“I would explicitly state the remaining stale window.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: is a delayed second delete a proof of correctness?
No; an unusually slow reader can still arrive after both deletes.
It may reduce the chance of stale fills, but timing is not coordination.
Choose it only with an honest bounded-risk explanation and a recovery policy.

quiz.question: Why can stale data reappear after a successful delete?
options: An earlier reader fills the cache later
quiz.explanation: The read and fill straddle the writer’s commit and invalidation.

quiz.question: What should a version-aware cache reject?
options: Updates older than the known version
quiz.explanation: A monotonic version comparison can prevent out-of-order data from replacing newer values.

quiz.question: Does a delayed second delete guarantee freshness?
options: No; slow readers can outlast the delay
quiz.explanation: Fixed timing does not prove that all concurrent stale fills have finished.

lessons.title: News feed: start with the read model
lessons.summary: Social news feed · Part 1 of 3: requirements & baseline.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a home feed for people who follow other users.
Ask whether the feed is chronological or ranked.
Assume chronological ordering, follow relationships, and durable posts first.
Leave recommendations and ads outside the initial scope.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A user’s feed combines posts from many authors.
Following one person is different from following tens of thousands.
Privacy changes and deleted posts must affect what readers can see.
A precomputed timeline is a derived index, not the source of ownership truth.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Store posts separately from follow relationships.
Start by fetching recent posts from followed authors and merging them.
Use cursor pagination with a stable ordering tie-breaker.
Fetch full post content after selecting candidate IDs and recheck visibility.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The reader supplies a cursor identifying the next time-and-ID boundary.
The feed service finds candidates from the follow graph.
It merges, filters, and returns a page with another opaque cursor.
A cursor avoids offset shifts, but does not by itself freeze a changing feed.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would begin with a chronological feed to make scope explicit.”
“Posts and follows are authoritative; timeline entries are derived.”
“I’d use cursor pagination and enforce visibility at read time.”
“Then I’d estimate whether fan-out on read is affordable.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why not use page number and offset?
New posts inserted ahead of a page shift its offsets.
Users may see duplicates or miss items while scrolling.
A cursor gives a stable boundary; a snapshot is an extra guarantee if required.

quiz.question: Why retain a separate authoritative post store?
options: Timeline entries are derived and may be stale
quiz.explanation: The source record owns content and visibility; a timeline is an access structure.

quiz.question: What does a stable tie-breaker help with?
quiz.explanation: A total ordering such as timestamp plus ID makes pagination boundaries unambiguous.

quiz.question: Does cursor pagination automatically provide a frozen snapshot?
options: Only if the cursor is shorter
No; snapshot semantics require additional design
quiz.explanation: Cursors describe a position; they do not necessarily preserve the exact underlying result set.

lessons.title: News feed: choose where fan-out happens
lessons.summary: Social news feed · Part 2 of 3: scaling & skew.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The interviewer adds millions of users and a few celebrity accounts.
Most authors have hundreds of followers; a few have tens of millions.
One uniform fan-out policy can become disproportionately expensive.
Separate the ordinary case from the heavy tail.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Fan-out on read merges author streams every time someone opens the feed.
Fan-out on write inserts a post ID into followers’ timelines upfront.
Read-time work saves writes, but can make feed opens expensive.
Write-time work makes reads cheap, but celebrities create enormous bursts.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a hybrid policy based on follower counts and activity.
Precompute ordinary authors into follower timelines.
Merge celebrity posts at read time instead of copying them to everyone.
Keep timeline entries compact and bounded; fetch content from the post store.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A new ordinary post enters an asynchronous fan-out queue.
Workers add its ID to follower timelines with duplicate-safe inserts.
Feed reads combine those entries with selected high-fan-out author streams.
If precomputation lags, freshness degrades visibly rather than corrupting source posts.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would explain both fan-out costs before choosing a hybrid.”
“Celebrity skew matters more than the average follower count.”
“The timeline cache stores IDs, not copies of every full post.”
“I’d measure fan-out lag and feed-open latency separately.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should inactive users receive every precomputed update?
That can waste storage and write bandwidth for timelines nobody reads.
Precompute for active readers and rebuild or merge when others return.
This saves resources but adds complexity to the first read after inactivity.

quiz.question: Which workload makes write fan-out costly?
options: A celebrity with millions of followers
quiz.explanation: One source write can expand into millions of derived timeline writes.

quiz.question: What is the point of hybrid fan-out?
options: Match read and write costs to skewed author traffic
quiz.explanation: A hybrid avoids forcing the expensive tail of the distribution into the same strategy as ordinary authors.

quiz.question: What should a fan-out lag metric describe?
options: Delay until posts appear in derived timelines
quiz.explanation: Queue and processing lag reveal freshness degradation even when post writes succeed.

lessons.title: News feed: ranking, deletion & late work
lessons.summary: Social news feed · Part 3 of 3: correctness & evolution.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Now add ranking and deletion to the feed.
A user deletes a post while old fan-out jobs are still queued.
Another user blocks the author after a timeline entry was created.
Derived entries can outlive the permissions that originally allowed them.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Deleting one cache entry cannot remove every stale timeline reference.
Retries may also reinsert a reference after a deletion event.
Ranking changes order, which complicates multi-page continuity.
A high-ranking candidate is not automatically an authorized candidate.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Keep durable tombstones or versioned deletion state where necessary.
Filter candidates against current visibility before returning content.
Make fan-out jobs idempotent and reject stale versions when applicable.
For ranked pagination, retain a ranking session or accept documented refresh behavior.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Candidate generation retrieves a bounded set of potentially relevant IDs.
Authorization removes unavailable, blocked, or deleted posts.
A ranker scores the remaining candidates within a latency budget.
A simple fallback ordering serves the feed if ranking is unavailable.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would separate candidate generation, authorization, and ranking.”
“Deletion is enforced through source visibility, not just cache cleanup.”
“I’d make late fan-out work unable to resurrect visible deleted content.”
“A chronological fallback keeps ranking failure from blanking the feed.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can stale references remain in internal storage?
Yes, temporarily, if they cannot expose deleted content and policy allows it.
Background cleanup removes them to control cost and retention.
User-facing deletion guarantees and physical retention requirements need separate definitions.

quiz.question: What prevents a stale timeline reference exposing a deleted post?
options: A current visibility check on the source state
quiz.explanation: Derived references can remain stale; access decisions must still enforce authoritative deletion and permissions.

quiz.question: What should happen when a ranker times out?
options: Use a defined safe fallback order
quiz.explanation: Ranking can degrade independently while visibility checks remain mandatory.

quiz.question: Why can ranked pagination need a session or snapshot?
options: Every post must use the same ID
Rankings can change between page requests
quiz.explanation: A consistent candidate sequence reduces duplicates and omissions caused by reordering between pages.

lessons.title: Chat: separate send from delivery
lessons.summary: Messaging service · Part 1 of 3: api & message lifecycle.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design one-to-one chat with offline delivery.
Clarify text versus media, group chat, retention, and read receipts.
Start with text messages, reconnecting clients, and durable history.
A persistent connection helps live delivery but does not replace storage.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
“Sent,” “delivered,” and “read” are different states.
A socket write does not prove the recipient saw the message.
The sender may disconnect immediately after sending.
The system needs an authoritative acknowledgement and a retry identity.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Accept a client-generated message ID scoped to its sender or conversation.
Persist the message before acknowledging durable acceptance.
Use a connection gateway for online recipients and history sync for offline ones.
Track recipient delivery acknowledgements separately from optional read receipts.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The sender submits a message through the gateway.
The message service stores it and returns its stable identity.
Online delivery is attempted; disconnected recipients catch up later.
The client can show accepted, delivered, and read without claiming more than it knows.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d define each user-visible message state first.”
“The server acknowledgement means persisted acceptance, not human reading.”
“A stable client message ID makes reconnect retries deduplicable.”
“Live sockets are an optimization over durable message history.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should a gateway hold all chat history in memory?
No; process restarts would destroy that history.
Gateways hold connection state, while durable storage owns messages.
Clients recover from disconnections by synchronizing from a known position.

quiz.question: What should a durable send acknowledgement mean?
options: The message has been accepted into durable storage
The recipient has definitely read it
quiz.explanation: Acceptance, delivery, and reading are separate states with different evidence.

quiz.question: Why include a client message ID?
options: To recognize repeated sends after reconnect
quiz.explanation: A stable operation identity allows retries to map to the same stored message.

quiz.question: Why are WebSockets alone insufficient?
options: Offline recipients need durable history and catch-up
quiz.explanation: A live connection transports data but does not supply persistence or offline synchronization.

lessons.title: Chat: order within a conversation
lessons.summary: Messaging service · Part 2 of 3: partitioning & ordering.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Two people send messages at nearly the same moment.
Different gateway servers receive their messages.
The interviewer asks whether every participant sees the same order.
Choose the scope of ordering before proposing a global sequence.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Device clocks can disagree and messages can arrive late.
Sorting solely by client timestamp can reorder a conversation unexpectedly.
A global sequencer for every conversation creates unnecessary coordination.
Most chat products need conversation-local ordering rather than one worldwide order.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Route a conversation’s writes through an owning partition or sequencer.
Assign a monotonically increasing conversation sequence at durable acceptance.
Use that sequence for history pagination and catch-up positions.
Preserve the client timestamp only as supplemental display metadata.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Gateways forward writes using the conversation partition key.
The owner appends accepted messages in one ordered history.
Delivery can be retried and arrive out of order at a device.
The client buffers or refetches gaps using server-assigned sequence positions.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d guarantee ordering per conversation, not across unrelated chats.”
“I wouldn’t rely on device clocks to define that order.”
“A partition owner assigns positions during the accepted write path.”
“Clients detect gaps and recover from durable history.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what happens when ownership changes?
Two active owners must not both assign conflicting accepted positions.
Use a leader epoch or fencing mechanism during failover.
Reject stale-owner writes; availability may pause while ownership is resolved.

quiz.question: What is the useful ordering scope for this design?
options: Only messages from one UI tab
quiz.explanation: Conversation-local order matches the product while avoiding unnecessary global coordination.

quiz.question: Why not trust client timestamps as the sole ordering source?
options: Clocks can differ and messages can arrive late
quiz.explanation: Client time does not provide a trustworthy distributed total order.

quiz.question: What protects ordering when ownership changes?
options: Epochs or fencing that reject stale owners
Allowing both owners to assign freely
quiz.explanation: Failover must prevent overlapping owners from accepting conflicting sequences.

lessons.title: Chat: reconnect without losing the thread
lessons.summary: Messaging service · Part 3 of 3: recovery & presence.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A phone loses connectivity for twenty minutes, then reconnects.
Live notifications were missed, and some sends have uncertain outcomes.
The user expects history to recover without duplicate messages.
Treat reconnect as a normal protocol, not a rare exception.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A transient delivery event can be lost even when a message is stored.
Presence can become stale after silent network failure.
Clients may reconnect to different gateways.
Neither gateway memory nor “online” status proves delivery.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Keep a durable or client-retained last-received sequence per conversation.
Fetch messages after that position when reconnecting.
Deduplicate resent outgoing messages using their stable operation IDs.
Expire presence with heartbeats and TTLs; describe it as approximate.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The reconnecting device authenticates and opens a new connection.
It requests history since its last contiguous received position.
It merges messages by ID and advances the cursor only after storing them.
Live delivery resumes; overlap with history sync is harmless after deduplication.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d use durable history as the recovery mechanism.”
“The reconnect cursor refers to a contiguous received prefix.”
“I would expect overlap between replay and live delivery.”
“Presence is a best-effort hint, not a delivery guarantee.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why not advance the cursor to the largest seen sequence?
An out-of-order message can arrive while an earlier message is still missing.
Advancing past that hole can skip the missing message during recovery.
Track contiguous progress or explicitly request missing ranges.

quiz.question: Why use the last contiguous position rather than the maximum seen?
options: To avoid skipping gaps during reconnect
To make every message globally ordered
quiz.explanation: A larger sequence may arrive before an earlier one; contiguous progress preserves the recovery boundary.

quiz.question: Does an online presence indicator guarantee delivery?
quiz.explanation: Heartbeats indicate recent connectivity, not successful acceptance by a specific device.

quiz.question: How should overlapping replay and live events be handled?
quiz.explanation: Overlap is expected during synchronization; a stable identity makes merging safe.

lessons.title: Notifications: turn events into intent
lessons.summary: Notification platform · Part 1 of 3: preferences & durable work.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design email, push, and SMS notifications for an online store.
Ask whether messages are transactional, promotional, or both.
Clarify opt-outs, urgency, supported channels, and quiet hours.
Assume an order-shipped event should notify a customer through allowed channels.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
An event says something happened; it does not specify every delivery decision.
A customer may disable promotions but still need transactional updates.
Provider calls are slow and can fail independently.
Calling all providers inside the order request couples unrelated failures.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Create a durable notification intent from the business event.
Resolve the recipient, template version, channel policy, and event identity.
Queue channel-specific work and track its lifecycle separately.
Recheck applicable preferences near delivery when delayed work can become invalid.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The order service commits its change with an outbox event.
A consumer turns that event into deduplicated notification intents.
Email, push, and SMS workers consume their own delivery work.
The customer-facing order flow does not wait for provider responses.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d separate business events from notification delivery intents.”
“Preferences and message category determine which channels are eligible.”
“Each intent has a stable identity and an observable status.”
“Separate workers isolate a failing provider from other channels.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why record the template version?
A retry should not unexpectedly change the promised message content.
Versioning also makes support and incident investigation more reproducible.
Avoid storing unnecessary sensitive data just to reconstruct a message.

quiz.question: Why distinguish an event from an intent?
options: Delivery policy adds recipient, channel, and template decisions
quiz.explanation: A business event is translated into one or more concrete, policy-aware delivery tasks.

quiz.question: Why separate channel workers?
options: All channels have identical failure modes
It removes the need for preferences
One provider outage should not block every channel
quiz.explanation: Independent queues and workers limit cross-channel failure propagation.

quiz.question: What does template versioning help with?
quiz.explanation: A stable template reference explains which content was used for a specific attempt.

lessons.title: Notifications: retries without a spam storm
lessons.summary: Notification platform · Part 2 of 3: delivery semantics.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The SMS provider times out after accepting a request.
Your worker cannot tell whether the message was sent.
Retrying might produce a duplicate; dropping it might lose delivery.
Explain this uncertainty instead of promising exactly-once messaging casually.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Local deduplication only stops duplicate work you can recognize internally.
A remote side effect may already have happened before a timeout.
The provider’s idempotency support determines how safely you can retry.
A queue acknowledgement must also reflect durable local progress.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a stable provider idempotency key when supported.
Persist attempts and provider references for reconciliation.
Retry transient errors with exponential backoff, jitter, and a deadline.
Route exhausted or permanent failures to inspection rather than retrying forever.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A worker claims an intent and records its current attempt.
It calls the provider with the same delivery identity across retries.
On a definitive response, it persists the outcome before acknowledging work.
After an ambiguous response, it queries status or retries under the provider contract.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would distinguish an internal duplicate from an uncertain external effect.”
“Provider idempotency makes safe retries much easier.”
“Without it, I’d state the duplicate-versus-loss tradeoff explicitly.”
“My design includes reconciliation, not just a retry loop.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should every 4xx response be retried?
No; invalid addresses or malformed requests need correction, not repetition.
Some rate-limit responses may be transient and include retry guidance.
Classify errors by meaning rather than using one policy for all status codes.

quiz.question: A provider times out after accepting work. What is known?
quiz.explanation: The response can be lost after the provider performs the side effect.

quiz.question: Which capability most improves safe provider retries?
options: A stable idempotency key honored by the provider
A new key for every attempt
quiz.explanation: The provider can recognize repeated requests as the same delivery operation.

quiz.question: What should happen to a permanently invalid destination?
options: Mark it failed and route it for correction if needed
quiz.explanation: Permanent errors require a terminal outcome or correction rather than endless transient retry behavior.

lessons.title: Notifications: protect urgent messages
lessons.summary: Notification platform · Part 3 of 3: scheduling & fairness.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A marketing campaign creates ten million pending notifications.
Password resets and security messages arrive at the same time.
One FIFO queue can leave urgent messages waiting behind the campaign.
The interviewer asks how you protect both latency and provider quotas.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Different classes of messages have different deadlines and business value.
Providers also enforce per-account or per-channel sending limits.
Adding workers can increase throttling without improving useful throughput.
Strict priority alone can starve low-priority work indefinitely.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use separate queues and capacity budgets for urgent and bulk work.
Apply provider-aware rate limits and bounded concurrency.
Choose weighted scheduling so bulk work still makes progress.
Expire obsolete messages rather than sending stale reminders much later.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A scheduler releases due intents into the appropriate priority lane.
Workers consume according to channel capacity and fairness policy.
Each delivery rechecks expiration and relevant user preferences.
Metrics track queue age by class, not just the total message count.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would isolate transactional delivery from bulk campaigns.”
“Queue age matters more than total depth for user-visible deadlines.”
“More workers do not overcome an external provider quota.”
“I’d reserve urgent capacity and prevent indefinite bulk starvation.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: how do quiet hours work across time zones?
Store the user’s time zone and schedule in local calendar semantics.
Time-zone changes and daylight-saving transitions can move delivery windows.
Recompute eligibility at delivery rather than trusting one old UTC timestamp blindly.

quiz.question: Which metric reveals delayed password resets?
options: Queue age for the urgent class
quiz.explanation: Class-specific waiting time exposes latency failures hidden by an aggregate backlog metric.

quiz.question: Why might more workers fail to raise delivery throughput?
options: The provider quota is the bottleneck
quiz.explanation: External sending limits constrain successful work regardless of local concurrency.

quiz.question: What is a drawback of strict priority scheduling?
options: All jobs become the same priority
quiz.explanation: Weighted policies can preserve urgent capacity while ensuring some progress for other classes.

lessons.title: File storage: separate bytes from metadata
lessons.summary: Cloud file storage · Part 1 of 3: upload protocol.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a service for uploading and sharing large files.
Clarify maximum size, resumability, access permissions, and retention.
Assume private files by default and intermittent mobile connections.
Avoid sending every file byte through your application workers unnecessarily.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Large uploads consume bandwidth, memory, and long-lived connections.
An upload can finish storing bytes while metadata publication fails.
A filename alone is not a safe identity or authorization boundary.
The system must distinguish incomplete uploads from visible files.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Keep file ownership and state in a metadata database.
Store bytes in object storage under generated object keys.
Issue short-lived, scoped upload authorizations after checking the user.
Finalize the file only after verifying the intended object and upload metadata.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The client requests an upload session from the API.
It uploads bytes directly using the session’s limited authorization.
A finalize call verifies the object and records the visible file version.
Download authorization is checked separately; possession of an ID is insufficient.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would separate the data plane from the metadata control plane.”
“The API grants scoped access; object storage handles the heavy bytes.”
“A file is visible only after a validated finalize transition.”
“Private download links are time-bounded capabilities, not permanent public paths.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what prevents an upload URL from being reused forever?
Limit its lifetime, target object, permitted operation, and applicable size constraints.
A leaked capability remains useful within those bounds.
Use suitable policy checks and avoid logging secret-bearing signed URLs.

quiz.question: Why upload bytes directly to object storage?
options: To avoid routing all large payloads through API workers
quiz.explanation: A separate byte-transfer path reduces application bandwidth and connection pressure.

quiz.question: When should a file become visible?
quiz.explanation: Finalization confirms that the expected bytes exist and metadata can reference them safely.

quiz.question: Does an unguessable file ID replace authorization?
options: Yes if it is long enough
quiz.explanation: Access checks are still required; identifiers can leak through logs, links, or shared context.

lessons.title: File storage: resume, version & sync
lessons.summary: Cloud file storage · Part 2 of 3: multipart & concurrency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A user uploads a 5 GB video over an unreliable connection.
Restarting the entire upload after each interruption is frustrating.
Another device may replace the same file during the upload.
You need resumable transport and an explicit version conflict policy.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A single giant request makes recovery expensive.
Blind last-write-wins can overwrite changes from another device.
A storage ETag is not universally a content checksum, especially for multipart uploads.
Integrity checks must follow the actual storage API contract.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Split the upload into numbered parts within one upload session.
Track accepted parts and retry missing ones with bounded concurrency.
Use explicit checksums where supported to validate content integrity.
Finalize against an expected metadata version using compare-and-swap semantics.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The client requests the upload’s current accepted-part list.
It sends only missing parts and completes the multipart object.
The metadata update includes the version the client originally edited.
A mismatch returns a conflict or creates a separate version instead of silently overwriting.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would solve transfer recovery and edit conflicts independently.”
“Multipart upload makes retransmission proportional to missing parts.”
“Optimistic concurrency protects metadata from a stale editor.”
“I’d use a documented checksum mechanism rather than assume ETag means MD5.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should chunk deduplication be global across tenants?
It can save bytes but can reveal whether another tenant owns particular content.
It also adds reference counting, encryption, and garbage-collection complexity.
Start with per-file resumability before adding cross-user deduplication.

quiz.question: What reduces retransmission after a dropped large upload?
quiz.explanation: Multipart state lets the client continue from accepted pieces rather than from the beginning.

quiz.question: How can a stale client avoid overwriting a newer version?
options: Finalize with an expected metadata version
quiz.explanation: A conditional update detects conflicting changes and can return an explicit conflict.

quiz.question: Is every object ETag a whole-file MD5 checksum?
options: No; semantics depend on the storage operation
Only when the file is private
quiz.explanation: Use the provider’s documented integrity mechanism rather than infer checksum meaning from the field name.

lessons.title: File storage: clean up without deleting live files
lessons.summary: Cloud file storage · Part 3 of 3: lifecycle & recovery.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Uploads succeed partially, clients disappear, and files are deleted later.
The interviewer asks how you avoid endless orphaned storage.
At the same time, cleanup must not delete bytes a user just finalized.
Treat garbage collection as a concurrent workflow, not a blind sweep.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Metadata and object storage are different systems with different failure points.
An uploaded object may exist without a completed metadata reference.
A deleted file may still have an active download capability.
Physical deletion and immediate access revocation are separate guarantees.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Give upload sessions explicit states and expiration times.
Use a grace period and conditional state transitions before cleanup.
Retain object versions or references until the deletion policy permits removal.
For strict access revocation, short-lived signed URLs alone may not be sufficient.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A sweeper finds expired unfinished sessions and claims them conditionally.
Finalization rejects sessions already marked for cleanup.
Cleanup removes abandoned parts or objects and records completion.
Retries are safe because deleting an already-removed object is treated as complete.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would model pending, finalized, and cleanup states explicitly.”
“The sweeper and finalizer must not both win the same transition.”
“I’d separate user-visible deletion from physical retention requirements.”
“A signed URL’s lifetime is part of the revocation contract.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: how would you prove backups are useful?
Define recovery point and recovery time objectives for metadata and bytes.
Exercise restoration operationally and maintain compatible version references.
A backup that exists but cannot restore a coherent file set is not enough.

quiz.question: What prevents a cleanup/finalize race?
quiz.explanation: Both operations must coordinate on whether the upload is still eligible for finalization.

quiz.question: Does deleting metadata instantly revoke an already-issued download URL?
options: Not necessarily; the capability may remain valid
Only if the filename is short
quiz.explanation: A storage capability can continue working until it expires or its target/access policy changes.

quiz.question: What makes cleanup retries safe?
options: Issuing new file IDs each attempt
Treating already-removed objects as completed work
quiz.explanation: Idempotent cleanup allows recovery after a crash between deletion and status recording.

lessons.title: Video: upload once, prepare many renditions
lessons.summary: Video streaming · Part 1 of 3: ingestion pipeline.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a video platform that supports mobile playback.
Ask whether the problem is live streaming or uploaded video.
Assume uploaded videos first, with several quality levels.
Separate ingestion from playback because their resource needs differ greatly.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
The original file may be too large or incompatible with a viewer’s device.
Transcoding is CPU- or GPU-intensive and can take minutes.
A successful upload does not mean every playback rendition is ready.
The UI needs states such as processing, ready, and failed.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Store the original object durably and enqueue a processing job.
Create segmented renditions at selected resolutions and bitrates.
Publish a manifest only when its referenced required segments exist.
Track pipeline state in metadata rather than inferring it from queue disappearance.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Upload finalization emits a durable processing intent.
Workers transcode into versioned output locations.
A validation/finalization stage marks the playable version ready.
Playback APIs return only a manifest whose readiness and access policy are satisfied.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d split the upload, processing, and playback paths.”
“An asynchronous pipeline fits work that exceeds interactive request budgets.”
“Output readiness is an explicit metadata transition.”
“I would not expose a manifest that points at incomplete required segments.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should one failed high-resolution rendition block all playback?
That depends on the minimum supported playback policy.
A low-resolution rendition can become ready before optional higher qualities.
The manifest can evolve under a versioned publication strategy.

quiz.question: Why use an asynchronous transcoding pipeline?
options: Processing can exceed an interactive request budget
It removes the need to store the source
quiz.explanation: Durable background work separates heavy processing from the user’s upload request.

quiz.question: When is a manifest safe to publish?
options: Immediately after creating a queue message
When required referenced segments are ready
quiz.explanation: A published manifest should refer to playable assets under the chosen readiness policy.

quiz.question: Does successful upload imply successful playback preparation?
options: Only if the upload used HTTPS
No; processing has its own lifecycle
quiz.explanation: Stored source bytes and ready playback renditions are separate states.

lessons.title: Video: serve viewers near the edge
lessons.summary: Video streaming · Part 2 of 3: cdn & adaptive playback.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Millions of viewers start the same popular video.
Sending every segment from the origin would waste bandwidth and overload it.
Some viewers have fast Wi-Fi; others move between weak mobile networks.
Design for shared content and changing bandwidth.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A single fixed bitrate either wastes quality or causes buffering.
The origin should not handle every repeated segment download.
A cold CDN still sends misses to upstream storage.
Popularity spikes can overwhelm the origin during initial cache fill.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use adaptive bitrate playback with multiple prepared renditions.
Deliver immutable, versioned segments through a CDN.
Let the player select quality based on observed throughput and buffer state.
Protect cold misses using origin shielding, caching policy, and bounded source capacity.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The client obtains an authorized manifest from the control plane.
It requests segments from a nearby CDN edge.
Cached segments are served locally; misses fetch from upstream.
The player can switch quality at supported segment boundaries as conditions change.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d cache the large immutable media path aggressively.”
“The manifest and authorization path have different freshness needs.”
“Adaptive bitrate is a client playback decision over prepared choices.”
“I’d size the origin for cold starts, not just steady cache hits.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can private content still use a CDN?
Yes, if access is enforced with suitable signed requests or edge authorization.
Do not cache personalized authorization responses as universally public data.
A token’s expiration and cache-key policy must match the security model.

quiz.question: Who typically chooses among prepared playback bitrates?
options: The player using network and buffer observations
quiz.explanation: The client adapts segment requests as measured conditions change.

quiz.question: Why version immutable segment URLs?
options: To make all content private by itself
quiz.explanation: A new asset version gets a new identity, avoiding ambiguity about cached bytes.

quiz.question: What load must still be considered with a CDN?
options: No origin traffic under any circumstance
quiz.explanation: Misses and cache-fill spikes still reach upstream systems.

lessons.title: Video: retry processing without corrupt publication
lessons.summary: Video streaming · Part 3 of 3: idempotent workflows.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A transcoding worker crashes after writing half its output.
The queue redelivers the job to another worker.
Both workers may briefly run if the first was only slow.
The interviewer asks how retries avoid mixed or partial published output.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Writing every attempt into the same mutable output directory is risky.
A stale worker can overwrite a newer attempt’s results.
Queue delivery does not guarantee one active attempt at every instant.
Publication needs a stronger ownership boundary than worker optimism.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Write output under an attempt or generation-specific prefix.
Use leases for recovery and fencing tokens for authoritative state changes.
Publish the completed generation through an atomic metadata pointer update.
Garbage-collect abandoned generations after a safe grace period.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A worker claims a job with an attempt identity and lease.
It writes rendition segments to its isolated generation.
After validation, it conditionally publishes only if its ownership is still valid.
Late workers cannot replace the active published generation with stale output.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would separate producing output from publishing it.”
“Each attempt writes isolated artifacts so partial work is harmless.”
“A conditional publish chooses one valid complete generation.”
“Retries may repeat computation, but they must not corrupt visible playback.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what metrics reveal pipeline health?
Measure queue age, processing duration, failure rate, and time-to-playable.
Break these down by codec, input duration, and rendition policy.
A high job success rate can still hide unacceptable waiting time.

quiz.question: Why isolate outputs by attempt?
options: To keep overlapping workers from mixing partial artifacts
To guarantee only one CPU instruction runs
quiz.explanation: Separate generations make failed or stale attempts safe to abandon.

quiz.question: What must a stale worker be unable to do?
options: Publish over a newer authorized generation
quiz.explanation: Fencing and conditional state changes protect the user-visible result even if computation continues.

quiz.question: Which metric captures the user’s wait after upload?
quiz.explanation: End-to-end readiness latency includes queueing and processing delays.

lessons.title: Search: build an index for the question
lessons.summary: Search service · Part 1 of 3: inverted index & retrieval.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design search for a product catalog with millions of items.
Clarify keyword matching, filters, typo tolerance, and ranking needs.
Start with text search plus category and price filters.
Separate authoritative product writes from a search-optimized read model.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Scanning every product for every search is too expensive.
A database row layout is not always optimized for text relevance.
Search results may lag behind recent product updates.
The product must define acceptable index freshness.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Build an inverted index mapping terms to matching document IDs.
Analyze text consistently during indexing and querying.
Intersect or combine candidate sets, apply filters, then rank candidates.
Store enough searchable fields to avoid fetching every source document during retrieval.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A product change enters a durable indexing pipeline.
The indexer updates the document’s searchable representation.
A query is analyzed into terms and retrieves candidate IDs.
Ranking and policy checks produce a bounded result page.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would explain the inverted index before naming a search engine.”
“The product database remains the source of truth.”
“Index freshness is an explicit service target.”
“I’d keep candidate retrieval distinct from relevance scoring.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why not run arbitrary substring checks on all records?
That work grows with the catalog size for each query.
An index pays preprocessing and storage costs to avoid repeated full scans.
The right index depends on the search behavior, not only the database brand.

quiz.question: What does an inverted index map?
options: Only IDs to raw image bytes
quiz.explanation: It supports finding documents containing terms without scanning the entire collection.

quiz.question: Which system owns authoritative product information?
quiz.explanation: The search index is a derived representation and may lag behind source changes.

quiz.question: What must be aligned between indexing and querying?
quiz.explanation: Compatible tokenization and normalization are needed for meaningful term matching.

lessons.title: Search: partition, retrieve, then rank
lessons.summary: Search service · Part 2 of 3: distributed query planning.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The catalog no longer fits comfortably on one search node.
Queries must search multiple partitions and return the best results.
The interviewer asks how to avoid moving every matching document.
Plan the amount of work at each stage.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Each shard can find many local matches for a broad query.
Sending all matches to one coordinator wastes bandwidth and memory.
A slow shard can dominate end-to-end query latency.
Scores and ranking features must be comparable under the chosen search engine semantics.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Have shards return bounded candidate sets with necessary ranking metadata.
A coordinator merges candidates and optionally reranks a larger shortlist.
Keep expensive model scoring out of the unbounded retrieval stage.
Use deadlines and define whether partial results are acceptable.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The coordinator sends the query and filters to relevant shards.
Each shard returns its local candidate set and execution status.
The coordinator merges and reranks a bounded pool.
It returns results plus any required indication of partial or degraded search.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would separate cheap retrieval from expensive reranking.”
“Candidate limits control fan-out cost but can affect recall.”
“I would measure shard tail latency, not just average query time.”
“Partial results are a product choice, not an invisible implementation trick.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does taking only local top ten always produce the best reranked global ten?
Not if the reranker uses signals absent from the local retrieval score.
A potentially great candidate can be discarded before reranking.
Increase the shortlist based on measured recall and latency tradeoffs.

quiz.question: Why bound candidates before expensive reranking?
options: To guarantee perfect recall for every query
quiz.explanation: Reranking is often costly, so a shortlist limits work while introducing a recall tradeoff.

quiz.question: Why can local top-ten retrieval miss the reranked global top ten?
options: The reranker may use different signals
quiz.explanation: A document with a modest retrieval score may have strong reranking features but never reach that stage.

quiz.question: What should a partial-shard failure policy specify?
options: Whether and how partial results are exposed
That all queries are always complete
quiz.explanation: The caller needs an honest contract about missing results or fallback behavior.

lessons.title: Search: rebuild without stale resurrection
lessons.summary: Search service · Part 3 of 3: index lifecycle.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A new tokenizer requires rebuilding the whole search index.
Product updates continue while the rebuild runs.
Switching to a stale snapshot would lose recent changes.
A rollback also needs a compatible versioned index strategy.
