cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Bulk indexing and live updates can race for the same document.
An old snapshot write may overwrite a newer event.
Deleted products can reappear if deletion information is discarded too early.
“Rebuild in the background” is incomplete without a change boundary.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Build a new versioned index from a known snapshot position.
Replay changes after that position using document versions.
Reject older updates and preserve deletion tombstones as needed.
Switch a logical alias only after catch-up and readiness criteria are satisfied.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The rebuild records a source snapshot or change-log boundary.
Bulk import populates the new index while subsequent changes are retained.
A replay phase catches it up and applies version-aware updates.
The read alias moves atomically to the new index; the old one remains briefly for rollback.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d combine a snapshot with a replayable change stream.”
“Document versions prevent old bulk records from winning late.”
“An alias switch separates index preparation from serving traffic.”
“Rollback must account for changes after the switch, not just keep old files.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: how long should old indexes remain?
Long enough for the rollback window and any active readers, within cost limits.
If the old index stops receiving changes, its freshness degrades immediately.
State that limitation before claiming rollback is instant and lossless.

quiz.question: What prevents late snapshot records replacing newer updates?
quiz.explanation: The target can reject updates older than the document version it already knows.

quiz.question: Why keep deletion information during a rebuild?
options: To prevent deleted documents from reappearing
quiz.explanation: A stale snapshot can contain a document whose later delete must still be applied.

quiz.question: What is required for a fresh rebuilt index?
options: Changing the alias before indexing starts
Catch-up from a known snapshot boundary
quiz.explanation: A reproducible boundary connects the initial snapshot to subsequent updates.

lessons.title: Ride matching: find nearby candidates
lessons.summary: Ride dispatch · Part 1 of 3: geospatial discovery.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a service that matches riders with nearby drivers.
Clarify whether the request is matching, pricing, navigation, or all three.
Start with location updates and assigning one available driver.
Assume matching should finish quickly, but exact global optimization is unnecessary.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Scanning every driver for every rider is expensive.
GPS data is noisy and driver locations become stale.
The nearest straight-line point may not be the fastest road arrival.
Discovery should produce candidates, not make the final assignment blindly.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Partition locations into geographic cells using a spatial index.
Search the rider’s cell and neighboring cells for recent available drivers.
Expand the radius when too few candidates are found.
Use road ETA or a suitable approximation to rank the bounded shortlist.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Drivers send timestamped location updates to the location service.
A rider request queries nearby cells with a freshness threshold.
The matcher scores a limited set of eligible drivers.
A separate reservation step attempts to claim one candidate.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d use the spatial index to narrow the search space.”
“Location freshness is part of eligibility, not just a map display detail.”
“Distance is a retrieval heuristic; ETA improves ranking.”
“Finding a nearby driver does not yet mean that driver is assigned.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why check neighboring cells?
A driver just across a cell boundary may be closer than one inside it.
Cell size trades lookup fan-out against candidate volume.
Choose and measure that tradeoff for the operating area and density.

quiz.question: Why search neighboring cells?
options: A nearby driver can lie across a cell boundary
quiz.explanation: Spatial partitions are indexing boundaries, not real-world distance barriers.

quiz.question: Why apply a location freshness threshold?
options: Old coordinates may no longer represent a usable candidate
quiz.explanation: A stale update can make an unavailable or distant driver appear nearby.

quiz.question: Is nearest straight-line distance always best?
options: Only if the database is sharded
No; road travel time can differ
quiz.explanation: Roads, direction, barriers, and traffic affect arrival time.

lessons.title: Ride matching: reserve one driver once
lessons.summary: Ride dispatch · Part 2 of 3: assignment invariants.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Two riders request the same available driver simultaneously.
Both matchers have a recent location and see “available.”
The system must avoid confirming incompatible assignments.
The difficult part is the state transition, not the distance calculation.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A read of availability can become stale before the write.
Multiple matchers may race using the same candidate snapshot.
A driver can also reject or fail to respond to an offer.
Assignment requires a lifecycle with timeout and ownership.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Model available, offered, accepted, and active-trip states.
Claim the driver with an atomic conditional transition from available.
Attach an offer ID and expiry; acceptance must reference that offer.
An expired or superseded offer cannot become an accepted assignment later.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A matcher attempts to reserve a candidate for a specific rider.
Exactly one conditional claim wins for that driver state.
The driver accepts within the lease window or the offer expires.
The rider receives confirmation only after the assignment transition commits.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would identify the invariant: one incompatible active assignment per driver.”
“A prior availability check does not enforce that invariant.”
“The claim must be atomic and tied to a specific offer.”
“Late acceptances must be rejected after the offer is no longer valid.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if the process crashes after claiming a driver?
The claim needs expiration or a recovery worker to avoid a permanent hold.
Recovery must not release a driver already transitioned into a real trip.
Use conditional state changes, not unconditional timeout cleanup.

quiz.question: What prevents two riders reserving the same driver?
options: A higher GPS update frequency alone
quiz.explanation: The shared state change, not the discovery snapshot, must enforce exclusivity.

quiz.question: Why include an offer ID in acceptance?
options: To reject acceptance of expired or replaced offers
quiz.explanation: Acceptance must be bound to the currently valid assignment attempt.

quiz.question: How should a timed-out reservation be released?
options: Only if it is still the same pending offer
quiz.explanation: Conditional cleanup avoids undoing a later accepted or active assignment.

lessons.title: Ride matching: hot cities & stale locations
lessons.summary: Ride dispatch · Part 3 of 3: regional scaling.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A stadium empties and thousands of riders request nearby cars.
The hotspot is geographically concentrated, not evenly distributed.
Drivers cross cell and region boundaries during the surge.
Explain how routing and stale updates affect both capacity and correctness.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Static geographic partitions can create one overloaded city cell.
Delayed location updates may place a driver in an old cell.
A partition split does not automatically resolve assignment ownership.
Location discovery can be eventually consistent while assignment cannot double-book.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use hierarchical cells or adaptive partitioning for dense areas.
Keep per-driver update versions so old location events do not overwrite newer ones.
Allow overlapping candidate discovery during movement and deduplicate by driver ID.
Route final assignment to the driver’s authoritative state owner.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Location updates maintain candidate indexes in relevant cells.
A matcher searches a bounded radius and filters stale entries.
Duplicate candidates collapse to one driver identity.
The assignment owner performs the conditional claim regardless of which cell found the driver.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d separate an approximate location index from authoritative assignment state.”
“A stale candidate may waste a claim attempt, but must not create a double booking.”
“City-level skew needs adaptive capacity, not just more global shards.”
“Location versions and driver IDs make movement and overlap manageable.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what should happen when no driver can be assigned?
Return an honest unavailable or retrying state with a bounded search policy.
Do not keep expanding search forever while the rider waits.
Monitor assignment latency and successful match rate by area, not only globally.

quiz.question: Which part may tolerate eventual consistency more easily?
quiz.explanation: Stale discovery can cause failed attempts; assignment must still preserve its exclusivity invariant.

quiz.question: Why use per-driver location versions?
quiz.explanation: Version ordering prevents delayed events from moving the indexed position backward in update history.

quiz.question: What metric can hide a stadium-area failure if viewed only globally?
quiz.explanation: A healthy worldwide average can mask severe local availability and latency problems.

lessons.title: Ticket booking: hold the seat, not the page
lessons.summary: Ticket booking · Part 1 of 3: inventory invariants.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design assigned-seat booking for a popular concert.
Clarify hold duration, payment timing, cancellations, and seat selection.
Assume one seat can belong to at most one confirmed booking.
A seat map is a display; the reservation store decides who owns a seat.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Many customers can click the same apparently available seat.
A cached seat map becomes stale immediately under contention.
Checking availability and then inserting a hold is a race.
The system must atomically decide which request wins.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Represent seats with available, held, and booked states.
Create a short-lived hold through a conditional update or transaction.
Record hold identity, owner, expiry, and a version for subsequent transitions.
Return a conflict when another valid hold or booking already owns the seat.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The browser selects a seat and requests a hold.
The reservation service atomically checks and claims that seat.
A successful response includes the hold ID and payment deadline.
The browser displays a countdown, but server time controls actual expiration.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d define the seat-ownership invariant before adding a queue.”
“The cached map is advisory; the reservation transaction is authoritative.”
“A hold is an expiring state, not a promise made by the UI.”
“Concurrent requests must have exactly one winning claim for that seat.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if a customer wants four adjacent seats?
Either reserve all required seats atomically or explicitly support partial holds.
Transactions spanning partitions may be costly, so partitioning by event can help.
Do not silently confirm only part of a group when the product promised all four.

quiz.question: What actually prevents double-booking?
quiz.explanation: Many clients can race; the authoritative shared-state operation must enforce exclusivity.

quiz.question: Which clock determines hold validity?
quiz.explanation: Client clocks and suspended tabs are unreliable enforcement mechanisms.

quiz.question: What is required for an all-or-nothing group reservation?
options: Confirming whichever seats happen to work
An atomic claim for the whole requested seat set
quiz.explanation: The implementation must match the promise that the group is reserved together or not at all.

lessons.title: Ticket booking: survive the opening minute
lessons.summary: Ticket booking · Part 2 of 3: admission & hot partitions.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A million fans arrive at the ticket-sale opening time.
Only a small fraction can reasonably contend for seats at once.
Scaling web servers alone increases pressure on the same inventory.
Protect the constrained write path before requests reach it.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
One event can be a hot partition despite a large overall database.
Repeated seat-map polling can overwhelm read capacity.
Bots and retries amplify the burst.
A waiting room controls admission; it does not itself prevent duplicate bookings.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a waiting room or bounded admission queue before reservation attempts.
Issue short-lived admission tokens and limit attempts per identity.
Serve approximate seat availability from a read-optimized path.
Keep reservation decisions on the authoritative transactional path.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The edge admits a controlled number of customers to checkout.
Clients browse cached availability and submit specific hold requests.
The inventory service accepts only capacity-bounded reservation traffic.
Rejected or queued clients receive clear retry guidance instead of retrying blindly.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would distinguish overload protection from inventory correctness.”
“Admission control keeps the reservation database inside its capacity envelope.”
“Seat-map reads can be approximate; seat claims cannot.”
“I’d measure successful holds and wait time, not just requests accepted at the edge.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does adding more shards solve one hot event?
Only if that event’s contention can be partitioned without breaking reservation needs.
Per-seat partitioning complicates multi-seat atomic claims.
Explain the tradeoff between locality for transactions and spreading write load.

quiz.question: Does a waiting room replace atomic seat claims?
options: Yes; queuing makes every write unique
No; it only controls traffic admission
quiz.explanation: Queue order and capacity control do not enforce the inventory ownership invariant.

quiz.question: Why can more API replicas make a sale worse?
options: They can send more concurrent work to the same bottleneck
quiz.explanation: Extra front-end capacity can amplify load on a constrained inventory write path.

quiz.question: What tradeoff arises when splitting one event across shards?
options: More distributed capacity but harder multi-seat transactions
quiz.explanation: Partition boundaries affect both contention and the scope of atomic reservation operations.

lessons.title: Ticket booking: payment after hold expiry
lessons.summary: Ticket booking · Part 3 of 3: cross-system recovery.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Payment succeeds just after the seat hold expires.
Another customer has already acquired the released seat.
The payment provider and reservation database cannot share a simple local transaction.
The system needs a policy for this conflict, not an optimistic success message.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A provider callback can be delayed, repeated, or arrive out of order.
Keeping holds forever protects payment completion but strands inventory.
Releasing holds promptly can race with a late successful payment.
There is no atomic cross-service action unless a coordination protocol provides one.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Define an order state machine linking hold, payment attempt, and booking.
Confirm the booking only if the hold is still valid and owned by that order.
If payment succeeded but the seat cannot be secured, initiate compensation.
Refund or void behavior depends on provider capabilities and the payment phase.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Payment events are authenticated, deduplicated, and persisted.
The handler conditionally converts the matching hold to a booking.
If conversion fails, the order enters a reconciliation or refund-needed state.
A recovery worker drives that state to completion and records the customer outcome.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would not equate payment success with booking success.”
“The final booking transition still checks the current hold owner.”
“Late payment without inventory needs an explicit compensation workflow.”
“I’d expose a pending state until the system has a coherent answer.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can extending the hold solve the whole problem?
It reduces one race but increases inventory lock time.
Extensions still require ownership checks and a bounded policy.
A reconciliation path remains necessary for ambiguous or delayed provider outcomes.

quiz.question: Payment succeeded after the seat was reassigned. What should happen?
options: Reconcile and compensate rather than double-book
quiz.explanation: The inventory invariant remains authoritative; money movement must be resolved through the defined compensation path.

quiz.question: Why must callbacks be deduplicated?
options: Providers may deliver the same event repeatedly
Every callback represents a new purchase
quiz.explanation: Repeated notifications should not cause repeated booking or refund effects.

quiz.question: Is a longer hold a complete correctness solution?
options: No; delayed and uncertain outcomes still exist
quiz.explanation: Longer leases change timing and capacity, but do not eliminate cross-system failures.

lessons.title: Payments: model the operation before the button
lessons.summary: Payment processing · Part 1 of 3: api & idempotency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a payment API for orders in a marketplace.
Clarify authorization, capture, refunds, currency, and provider responsibilities.
Assume an external processor performs the actual card charge.
Your application orchestrates and records payment state; it is not a card network.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A user can tap Pay twice or retry after a timeout.
Two different amounts must not silently share one idempotency identity.
Money should not use imprecise binary floating-point arithmetic.
A single boolean paid flag cannot describe all intermediate outcomes.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Accept an order ID and an idempotency key scoped to the customer.
Store a request fingerprint and return the prior result for matching retries.
Reject key reuse with a materially different request.
Represent amounts with explicit currency and appropriate exact units or decimal precision.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The API creates or retrieves a durable payment operation.
That operation references one provider attempt identity.
The order displays pending until a definitive outcome is recorded.
Authorized, captured, failed, and refunded states remain distinguishable.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would start with the payment lifecycle and retry contract.”
“Idempotency means the same intended operation, not merely the same endpoint.”
“A reused key with a different amount is an error.”
“The order and payment each have explicit states.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why not use a unique order ID as the only retry key?
An order may legitimately have multiple failed attempts or partial captures.
Operation identity should match the exact action being deduplicated.
Model a payment attempt under the order instead of conflating every future action.

quiz.question: A key is reused with a different amount. What should the API do?
quiz.explanation: Idempotency keys identify a stable intended request, so payload mismatches must be detected.

quiz.question: Why avoid a single paid boolean?
options: Every order uses only one network call
Payment has meaningful intermediate and reversal states
quiz.explanation: Authorization, capture, failure, refund, and uncertainty require a richer state model.

quiz.question: What is a safe money representation principle?
options: Ignore currency if the number is small
Use exact amounts with explicit currency semantics
quiz.explanation: Exact representation and currency-specific precision avoid accidental rounding and interpretation errors.

lessons.title: Payments: uncertain is a real state
lessons.summary: Payment processing · Part 2 of 3: external effects & webhooks.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A worker sends a charge request and loses the response.
The provider may have charged the customer successfully.
The application crashes before persisting any success state.
The interviewer asks what the next worker should do.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A database rollback cannot undo a completed external charge.
Creating a new provider identity on every retry risks multiple charges.
Webhook events may arrive before the original API response.
Both paths must converge on the same payment operation.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use the same provider idempotency identity for retries of one operation.
Persist provider references and treat ambiguous outcomes as pending or unknown.
Verify webhook authenticity and deduplicate by event identity.
Apply only valid state transitions; do not let a late event regress a final state.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A recovery worker finds unresolved payment operations.
It queries provider status or retries according to the provider’s contract.
Webhook and polling results update the same durable operation conditionally.
A definitive outcome triggers order processing through a durable event path.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would explicitly model uncertainty after a network timeout.”
“I’d reuse the provider operation key rather than create another charge.”
“Webhooks and reconciliation must share one state machine.”
“A local transaction alone cannot guarantee exactly-once external effects.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can an unsigned webhook mark an order paid?
No; anyone able to call the endpoint could forge it.
Verify the provider’s signature and relevant request details.
Still deduplicate verified events; authenticity does not imply single delivery.

quiz.question: After a charge timeout, what is the safe interpretation?
quiz.explanation: A response can be lost after the external action completes.

quiz.question: Why reuse the provider operation key?
options: To make a retry refer to the same intended charge
To create a fresh charge each time
quiz.explanation: Provider-side idempotency can prevent repeated side effects for one operation.

quiz.question: Why verify webhook signatures and deduplicate?
options: They address authenticity and repeated delivery separately
quiz.explanation: A genuine event can be repeated, and a unique-looking event can still be forged.

lessons.title: Payments: explain the ledger and reconciliation
lessons.summary: Payment processing · Part 3 of 3: auditability & invariants.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The marketplace must explain seller balances and refunds.
A mutable balance field is fast to read but weak as the only history.
The interviewer asks how finance can investigate discrepancies.
Build an auditable model instead of editing past amounts in place.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A displayed balance can diverge from provider settlement records.
Retries can duplicate accounting entries if identities are weak.
Correcting a historical entry by overwriting it destroys the original evidence.
Cross-currency arithmetic also needs an explicit conversion policy.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Record immutable, balanced journal entries with stable operation references.
Use compensating entries for corrections instead of rewriting history.
Derive or maintain balance projections transactionally from committed entries.
Reconcile internal operations against provider reports and unresolved settlements.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A captured payment produces a unique accounting transaction.
The ledger commits its balanced entries atomically.
A projection updates query-friendly balances from those entries.
A reconciliation job flags mismatches for resolution without inventing missing money.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d make the ledger an append-only explanation of money movement.”
“A cached balance is a projection, not the only financial evidence.”
“Corrections use compensating entries with traceable references.”
“Reconciliation checks our records against the external processor.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does double-entry bookkeeping guarantee business correctness?
No; an incorrect but balanced entry is still incorrect.
Authorization, amounts, account mapping, and deduplication also matter.
The ledger supplies strong accounting invariants and auditability, not magical correctness.

quiz.question: Why use compensating entries for corrections?
options: To erase all evidence of the original operation
quiz.explanation: A new correction preserves both the original event and the adjustment that explains the final balance.

quiz.question: What does reconciliation compare?
options: Internal records with external settlement or provider records
quiz.explanation: Independent records reveal missing, duplicated, or unresolved financial operations.

quiz.question: Does a balanced ledger guarantee every payment was valid?
options: No; balanced entries can still reflect wrong business inputs
quiz.explanation: Accounting balance is one invariant; authorization and correct business meaning require additional controls.

lessons.title: Analytics: capture useful events
lessons.summary: Event analytics · Part 1 of 3: event contracts.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design product analytics for clicks, searches, and purchases.
Ask whether the product needs real-time dashboards, audit history, or both.
Assume a dashboard with minute-level freshness and replayable raw events.
Define event meaning before selecting a streaming platform.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Clients retry, go offline, and have inaccurate clocks.
A click event and a confirmed purchase have different trust levels.
Unversioned event formats make downstream consumers brittle.
A raw stream without retention limits grows without bound.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Give each event an ID, type, schema version, and relevant subject identifiers.
Record event time and ingestion time separately.
Validate payloads and minimize sensitive fields at ingestion.
Retain raw events under an explicit policy so aggregates can be rebuilt.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The client or trusted service creates an event with a stable identity.
An ingestion endpoint validates it and writes to a durable stream.
Independent consumers build dashboards and archival storage.
Malformed events go to a controlled rejection path with observability.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d start with event semantics and the freshness requirement.”
“Client event time is useful, but ingestion time is a separate fact.”
“Confirmed purchases should come from a trusted business source.”
“Raw retention makes reprocessing possible within a defined window.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should every click block on a dashboard update?
No; ingestion durability and dashboard materialization are separate stages.
Blocking the product on analytics availability can harm core user actions.
Choose whether loss is acceptable per event class and expose ingestion failures honestly.

quiz.question: Why record both event time and ingestion time?
options: They answer different questions when events arrive late
quiz.explanation: Event time describes occurrence; ingestion time describes when the system received it.

quiz.question: Which source should confirm a purchase for revenue analytics?
options: The color of the checkout button
The trusted purchase or payment workflow
quiz.explanation: A UI interaction is not evidence of a completed business transaction.

quiz.question: Why retain raw events?
options: To support replay and aggregate correction within policy
To store data forever without a budget
quiz.explanation: Raw history allows derived views to be rebuilt, subject to retention and privacy constraints.

lessons.title: Analytics: late events change the answer
lessons.summary: Event analytics · Part 2 of 3: windows & deduplication.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Build a dashboard showing purchases per minute.
A mobile device reconnects and uploads events from twenty minutes ago.
The interviewer asks which minute should receive those events.
A processing-time counter and an event-time counter answer different questions.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Using ingestion time misattributes delayed activity to the reconnect minute.
Using event time requires a policy for late arrivals.
Retries can also count the same event twice.
A watermark is a progress estimate, not proof that no older event exists.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Choose event-time windows when the metric is about when actions happened.
Define allowed lateness and whether published windows can be corrected.
Deduplicate event IDs within a retention horizon appropriate to expected delays.
Route very late events to correction or separate reporting rather than silently guessing.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The processor groups events into their event-time minute.
It tracks progress and emits preliminary aggregates.
Late events within policy update or retract earlier results.
Downstream storage uses idempotent aggregate versions so repeated writes do not double-count.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d ask whether the dashboard values may be revised.”
“Watermarks make a useful latency-versus-completeness tradeoff.”
“Deduplication needs a bounded state-retention policy.”
“A final-looking number should not hide known late-event limitations.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can deduplication remember every event forever?
That requires unbounded storage and may violate retention requirements.
Choose the maximum supported replay or delay horizon deliberately.
Events outside that horizon need a documented policy and possibly offline correction.

quiz.question: What does a watermark represent?
options: A guarantee no older event can ever arrive
quiz.explanation: Watermarks guide when to emit or finalize windows under an explicit lateness policy.

quiz.question: Why can retries inflate purchase counts?
options: The same event may be processed more than once
Event IDs are always globally sorted
quiz.explanation: Duplicate delivery requires stable identity and deduplication or idempotent aggregation.

quiz.question: What tradeoff comes with a short allowed-lateness window?
options: Faster finalization but more events needing later correction
No need to store any state
quiz.explanation: Closing windows sooner reduces latency and state while excluding more delayed arrivals from the normal path.

lessons.title: Analytics: replay without double counting
lessons.summary: Event analytics · Part 3 of 3: recovery & schema evolution.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A bug incorrectly calculated revenue for the last three days.
Raw events are still retained and the team wants to rebuild aggregates.
Production ingestion continues during the correction.
A replay must not simply add the same purchases to existing totals.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Appending corrected counts into the same accumulator duplicates old effects.
A new schema may also make old consumers misinterpret fields.
The output store might not share the stream processor’s transaction boundary.
“Exactly once” must be scoped to the full source-to-sink path.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Build corrected results in a new generation or replace by stable window keys.
Use event IDs and deterministic transformations where practical.
Coordinate checkpoints with output commits using supported semantics.
Version schemas and define compatibility or explicit migration rules.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A replay reads from a specified source range or snapshot boundary.
The corrected processor writes a separate aggregate generation.
Live changes are caught up before the serving pointer moves.
Keep the old generation for a bounded rollback window and document freshness differences.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d rebuild derived data without incrementing the old totals again.”
“The replay boundary and output identity make the operation reproducible.”
“I would verify what exactly-once covers at the sink boundary.”
“Schema evolution is a contract across producers and consumers.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does Kafka alone guarantee an external SQL write occurs once?
No; the database side effect needs its own transaction or idempotency strategy.
Offsets and output changes must be coordinated or made replay-safe.
State the actual guarantee rather than borrowing the broker’s terminology broadly.

quiz.question: Why rebuild into a new generation?
options: To avoid mixing old and corrected aggregate effects
quiz.explanation: An isolated output makes comparison and controlled replacement possible without double-incrementing existing totals.

quiz.question: Does a broker guarantee exactly-once arbitrary external effects by itself?
quiz.explanation: The external sink must participate in compatible coordination or support idempotent effects.

quiz.question: What makes a replay reproducible?
options: A random new formula each run
A defined input boundary and deterministic output identity
quiz.explanation: Stable inputs and output keys make reruns understandable and safe to reconcile.

lessons.title: Job scheduler: claim work durably
lessons.summary: Background job platform · Part 1 of 3: state & ownership.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a background job service for report generation.
Clarify scheduled time, retry policy, cancellation, and execution duration.
Assume jobs must survive process restarts and may take several minutes.
Start with one durable job state machine rather than a fleet of timers.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A process-local timer disappears when its server restarts.
Two workers can discover the same due job simultaneously.
A worker can crash after claiming work but before completing it.
A permanent running flag can strand the job forever.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Store job payload reference, due time, state, attempt, and ownership lease.
Claim due jobs with an atomic operation appropriate to the store.
A worker periodically renews its lease while making progress.
Expired ownership makes the job eligible for controlled recovery.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The scheduler finds a bounded batch of due pending jobs.
A worker claims a job and records an attempt identity.
It executes the task and commits the result under that identity.
Successful completion transitions the job to done only if ownership is valid.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d make the durable job record the authority.”
“Claiming work is atomic, so competing workers cannot both own the same attempt.”
“A lease permits recovery after a crash.”
“I would still design the task for duplicate execution during failure.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why can a lease still allow overlapping execution?
A paused worker may continue after its lease expires and another worker starts.
A lease controls recognized ownership, not physical CPU execution.
Fencing and idempotent effects are needed to keep stale attempts harmless.

quiz.question: Why use a lease instead of a permanent running flag?
options: To recover work after a worker disappears
To guarantee no duplicate execution ever
quiz.explanation: Expiring ownership lets the system reclaim work that would otherwise remain stuck.

quiz.question: Why must job claiming be atomic?
options: Multiple workers can observe the same pending job
quiz.explanation: A read followed by an unguarded write allows competing workers to claim the same task.

quiz.question: Does lease expiration stop an old worker’s code automatically?
quiz.explanation: Ownership can expire while the original process continues running; its effects must be controlled separately.

lessons.title: Job scheduler: retries are additional load
lessons.summary: Background job platform · Part 2 of 3: backoff & fairness.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A downstream report service becomes unavailable.
Thousands of jobs fail and become eligible for retry.
Immediate retries can overwhelm the dependency just as it recovers.
The scheduler should make progress without becoming an outage amplifier.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Not every error is transient or safe to retry.
A bad input can fail forever while consuming capacity.
One tenant’s large backlog can delay everyone else.
Retry traffic competes with new work and needs its own budget.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Classify failures into retryable, terminal, and ambiguous outcomes.
Use exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt policy, and deadlines.
Apply per-tenant concurrency and fair selection among queues.
Send exhausted jobs to a durable inspection state rather than silently dropping them.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A failed attempt records its error category and next eligible time.
The scheduler waits until that time before offering another claim.
Admission respects both tenant budgets and downstream capacity.
Operators can inspect failed jobs and retry them deliberately after correction.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d treat retries as load that must fit within a capacity budget.”
“A terminal validation error should not enter an infinite loop.”
“Fairness prevents one tenant from monopolizing workers.”
“I would measure oldest runnable-job age by tenant and class.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should retrying a job always rerun every step?
No; expensive completed stages can be checkpointed when their outputs are durable.
A checkpoint must identify the exact input and output version.
Resume only from states whose side effects can be trusted or reconciled.

quiz.question: Why add jitter to retry delays?
options: To spread retries instead of synchronizing them
quiz.explanation: Randomized delay reduces retry herds that can overload a recovering dependency.

quiz.question: What should happen to a malformed report request?
options: A terminal failure with useful feedback
quiz.explanation: A permanent input error needs correction, not more attempts with identical input.

quiz.question: What does per-tenant concurrency protect?
options: Other tenants’ access to shared workers
The exact order of all global events
quiz.explanation: Fair resource budgets prevent a single tenant’s backlog from consuming every execution slot.

lessons.title: Job scheduler: cancellation is a protocol
lessons.summary: Background job platform · Part 3 of 3: fencing & deadlines.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A user cancels a report while its worker is paused.
The lease expires and another worker becomes eligible to retry.
The first worker resumes and tries to publish its output.
A cancellation flag alone cannot stop code already running elsewhere.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Cancellation can mean stop future work, stop compute, or suppress visible output.
External side effects may already have happened.
A stale worker may believe its ownership is still valid.
The product must define the latest point at which cancellation is guaranteed.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Record cancellation intent in the durable job state.
Workers check it at safe points and obey a total execution deadline.
Use an attempt token or generation check when committing visible results.
External irreversible effects need a separate cancellation or compensation contract.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The cancellation request changes the job state conditionally.
A worker stops cooperatively when it observes that state.
Any later result publication must still pass the current ownership and state check.
Cleanup removes abandoned outputs without exposing them as completed reports.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d define cancellation semantics before promising an instant stop.”
“Cooperative checks reduce wasted work but are not the final guard.”
“A conditional publish prevents stale or canceled attempts from becoming visible.”
“External effects require their own recovery policy.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if a report was already downloaded?
Cancellation cannot retract bytes already delivered to the user.
It can revoke future access under the file-serving policy.
Distinguish preventing future visibility from reversing an already-completed action.

quiz.question: What prevents a stale worker publishing after cancellation?
options: A conditional result commit against current state and attempt
Only the worker’s old in-memory flag
quiz.explanation: The authoritative state must still approve publication even if the worker missed a cancellation notification.

quiz.question: Does cancellation necessarily undo an external side effect?
options: Only if the job ID is numeric
quiz.explanation: An effect already performed may need compensation or may be irreversible.

quiz.question: Why use a total execution deadline?
options: To remove all need for state
To bound repeated work and waiting across attempts
quiz.explanation: A deadline caps the overall usefulness and resource budget of long-running work.

lessons.title: Metrics: a time series is a label set
lessons.summary: Monitoring platform · Part 1 of 3: data model & ingestion.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design metrics collection for thousands of services.
Clarify scrape versus push, dashboard freshness, retention, and alerting needs.
Assume numeric samples tagged by service, region, and status class.
Begin with the time-series identity and allowed label dimensions.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Each distinct metric name and label combination creates a separate series.
Adding user IDs or request IDs as labels can create enormous cardinality.
Storage cost depends on samples and series metadata, not just request volume.
A useful metric must aggregate along stable operational dimensions.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Represent samples with series identity, timestamp, and numeric value.
Enforce label and series limits at ingestion.
Store time-oriented chunks and indexes for permitted label queries.
Use logs or traces for high-cardinality request-specific details instead.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Collectors submit or expose samples with consistent labels.
Ingestion validates timestamps, labels, and tenant limits.
Samples are routed by series identity to storage shards.
Queries select series and aggregate values over a chosen time range.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would define cardinality budgets before choosing storage nodes.”
“A request ID belongs in traces or logs, not an unrestricted metric label.”
“Series identity determines partitioning and index cost.”
“Retention and resolution control long-term sample volume.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: is a small number of label names necessarily safe?
No; each label may have many values, and combinations multiply.
Ten labels with uncontrolled values can create a vast number of series.
Estimate actual distinct combinations rather than count label names alone.

quiz.question: What defines a distinct time series?
options: Metric name plus its label set
quiz.explanation: Different label combinations identify different streams of samples.

quiz.question: Why is request_id a risky metric label?
options: It can create nearly one series per request
quiz.explanation: Unbounded label values cause high series cardinality and index overhead.

quiz.question: What determines whether labels are affordable?
options: The font size of the chart
The number of distinct value combinations
Only the number of label names
quiz.explanation: Cardinality grows with actual combinations, which can be far larger than the label count.

lessons.title: Metrics: why you cannot average p99s
lessons.summary: Monitoring platform · Part 2 of 3: aggregation & retention.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The interviewer asks for global p99 latency across twenty instances.
Each instance already reports its own p99.
Averaging those twenty values seems convenient but gives the wrong statistic.
Percentiles are properties of a distribution, not additive counters.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Instances may handle radically different request counts.
A percentile summary loses information about the original distribution.
Even a request-weighted average of p99 values is generally not global p99.
Downsampling must preserve the information needed for future queries.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Collect compatible latency histograms or another mergeable distribution sketch.
Merge counts across instances before estimating the desired percentile.
Choose bucket boundaries or sketch accuracy for the latency range that matters.
Retain coarser aggregates longer, while documenting the queries they can still answer.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Each instance records latency observations into the agreed representation.
Storage retains bucket counters or sketch data with timestamps.
The query combines distributions over the requested instances and time window.
It estimates p99 from the combined distribution with the representation’s accuracy limits.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would never claim the average of per-instance p99s is global p99.”
“I need mergeable distribution information.”
“Histogram boundaries determine approximation quality near the target.”
“Long-term downsampling trades resolution and query flexibility for cost.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can bucket boundaries differ between instances?
Not if you intend to directly sum bucket counts as one histogram.
Align the representation or use a defined conversion with known information loss.
Changing histogram schema requires an explicit compatibility plan.

quiz.question: How should global p99 be computed from distributed observations?
options: Merge compatible distributions, then estimate p99
quiz.explanation: Percentiles cannot generally be aggregated by averaging already-computed percentiles.

quiz.question: What affects histogram percentile accuracy?
quiz.explanation: The distribution is approximated at bucket resolution, especially around the queried percentile.

quiz.question: What does downsampling trade away?
options: Fine-grained historical detail and some query options
quiz.explanation: Coarser retained data is cheaper but cannot answer every query that raw samples support.

lessons.title: Metrics: alert on symptoms that matter
lessons.summary: Monitoring platform · Part 3 of 3: slos & failure detection.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Your service has a 99.9% successful-request objective over a defined window.
The monitoring system sees a sudden rise in errors.
The interviewer asks when to page an engineer.
An alert should represent user harm and urgency, not every unusual graph.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A single failed request can trigger noise on a low-traffic service.
A long averaging window can hide a fast outage.
Missing telemetry is not the same as a measured zero error rate.
Alert delivery itself can fail and requires observable health.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Define the SLI numerator, denominator, and which requests are eligible.
Use error-budget burn rates across short and longer windows.
Require sufficient evidence or a deliberate low-traffic policy.
Track telemetry freshness separately from application success measurements.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The evaluator reads recent success and total request counts.
It calculates error rate and compares budget consumption over multiple windows.
Sustained urgent burn creates a deduplicated incident notification.
Recovery and silence rules prevent repeated pages for the same ongoing issue.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d start with a user-facing SLI and an explicit measurement window.”
“Burn rate expresses how fast we are consuming the allowed error budget.”
“Multiple windows balance fast detection against noise.”
“No data should trigger a separate interpretation, not automatic health.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what does 10× burn mean for a 99.9% success target?
The allowed error fraction is 0.1%, so 1% errors is a 10× rate under that definition.
It describes a rate relative to the budget, not ten failed requests.
Traffic eligibility and the evaluation window must remain consistent.

quiz.question: At a 0.1% allowed error fraction, what is 1% observed error rate?
quiz.explanation: Divide the observed 1% error fraction by the allowed 0.1%; the result is a relative rate.

quiz.question: What should missing telemetry mean?
options: Unknown measurement requiring its own policy
quiz.explanation: Missing evidence differs from measured success or measured failure.

quiz.question: Why combine short and long alert windows?
options: To balance rapid detection and noise resistance
quiz.explanation: Different windows provide evidence about both current severity and sustained impact.

lessons.title: Checkout: an order is a state machine
lessons.summary: E-commerce checkout · Part 1 of 3: api & ownership.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design checkout for a cart containing several products.
Clarify price guarantees, inventory reservations, shipping, and payment capture timing.
Assume the cart is editable until checkout begins.
The order becomes a durable record of the agreed purchase terms.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A cart is not an order, and an order is not a payment.
Prices can change while the customer is browsing.
Inventory can disappear before checkout completes.
A single synchronous chain can leave ambiguous partial success after a timeout.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Create an order with immutable line-item snapshots and an idempotency identity.
Record quantities, currency, price policy, and relevant product references.
Use explicit pending, reserved, paid, confirmed, and failed states as needed.
Define which service owns each transition and invariant.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The checkout API validates the cart and creates or retrieves the order.
It reserves inventory and initiates payment through durable workflow steps.
Only the required successful transitions allow final confirmation.
The client polls or receives an update for the same order after a timeout.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d separate mutable shopping intent from the durable purchase record.”
“An order stores what the customer agreed to buy at checkout.”
“A retry should return the same order operation, not create another purchase.”
“Confirmation means the required business invariants have been satisfied.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: why snapshot item names and prices in the order?
The product catalog can change after purchase.
Historical receipts should still explain the transaction that occurred.
Keep appropriate references too, but do not reconstruct every receipt from today’s catalog.

quiz.question: Why snapshot line-item prices in an order?
options: To preserve the purchase terms despite later catalog changes
quiz.explanation: Historical transaction meaning should not drift when the live catalog is edited.

quiz.question: What should a checkout retry reuse?
options: A new unrelated order every time
quiz.explanation: Idempotent operation identity avoids accidental duplicate purchases after uncertain responses.

quiz.question: Why distinguish cart, order, and payment?
options: They have different lifecycles and responsibilities
They must all share one boolean
quiz.explanation: Editable intent, a purchase record, and money movement each need their own semantics.

lessons.title: Checkout: coordinate with a saga
lessons.summary: E-commerce checkout · Part 2 of 3: cross-service consistency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Inventory reservation succeeds, but payment is declined.
Or payment succeeds and an order-confirmation worker crashes.
These steps live in separate services.
A local database transaction cannot atomically commit all of them.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Every step can complete while its acknowledgement is lost.
Blind rollback language hides the fact that external effects already happened.
Some actions can be undone; others need a new compensating action.
The workflow must remember which outcomes are known and which remain uncertain.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a durable orchestrated workflow or well-defined event choreography.
Give each step a stable identity and make retries idempotent.
Define compensation such as releasing inventory or refunding a captured payment.
Keep workflow state recoverable so crashes do not erase unfinished obligations.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The order coordinator requests an inventory reservation.
It proceeds to the selected payment phase after reservation succeeds.
A decline triggers inventory release; an uncertain charge triggers reconciliation.
Confirmation follows only when the required successful outcomes are established.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d call this a saga, then explain its actual states and compensations.”
“Compensation is a new business action, not a time machine.”
“Every step needs a retry identity and durable progress.”
“An ambiguous payment must be resolved before choosing the next transition.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: are events alone enough to make the workflow reliable?
No; state changes and emitted events can split during crashes.
Use an outbox or another supported atomic publication mechanism.
Consumers must still deduplicate and apply valid state transitions.

quiz.question: What is a compensation?
options: A guaranteed rewind of every system
A new action that counteracts an earlier business effect
quiz.explanation: Releasing a reservation or issuing a refund handles prior effects without pretending they never happened.

quiz.question: What should an uncertain payment trigger?
options: Reconciliation before an unsafe next step
quiz.explanation: The workflow must establish the actual outcome before making conflicting decisions.

quiz.question: Why persist workflow progress?
quiz.explanation: Durable state lets another worker resume or compensate without guessing what happened.

lessons.title: Checkout: prevent overselling at the source
lessons.summary: E-commerce checkout · Part 3 of 3: inventory concurrency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The last item is in stock and two customers check out together.
Both pages show quantity one.
The interviewer asks whether a fast Redis cache can solve this.
The real issue is coordinated inventory ownership, not lookup latency.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Two independent reads can both observe the final available unit.
A later decrement by each buyer can oversell.
Replica lag makes availability checks even less authoritative.
Reservation expiry can also race with order confirmation.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use an atomic conditional decrement or a transactional reservation model.
Require available quantity to cover the requested amount in the same operation.
Track reservations by order and make reserve/release idempotent.
Confirm or expire only the matching current reservation state.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Checkout requests a reservation for an order and quantity.
The inventory owner conditionally reduces available stock and creates the hold.
Payment success converts the hold to committed consumption.
Failure or expiry releases it once, without returning already-consumed stock.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would put the no-oversell invariant in the inventory write path.”
“A fast cache is useful for browsing, not sufficient for ownership.”
“Reservation and release both need idempotent identities.”
“I’d keep expiry conditional so it cannot undo a confirmed purchase.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what if inventory is split across warehouses?
Availability is scoped to actual fulfillment locations and allocation rules.
A global number can hide stock that cannot serve a particular order.
Reserve against a chosen fulfillment plan, or define a coordinated reallocation workflow.

quiz.question: What prevents overselling the last unit?
options: Waiting a fixed number of milliseconds
A conditional stock change within an atomic operation
Reading stock twice from a cache
quiz.explanation: The availability predicate and state mutation must be coordinated under concurrency.

quiz.question: Why must release be idempotent?
options: Duplicate release events must not create extra stock
quiz.explanation: Returning the same reserved quantity more than once inflates availability incorrectly.

quiz.question: Why can total global stock be misleading?
options: All warehouses always share one shelf
Some stock may not satisfy the order’s fulfillment constraints
quiz.explanation: Location, shipping, and allocation policy determine whether physical stock can fulfill this order.

lessons.title: Collaborative docs: define the convergence goal
lessons.summary: Collaborative editor · Part 1 of 3: operations & synchronization.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a document editor where several people type together.
Ask whether offline editing, rich text, and multi-device editing are required.
Start with a shared text document and a server-coordinated operation stream.
The main challenge is merging intent under concurrent edits.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Two users can insert text at the same numeric position.
Applying operations in different orders can produce different results.
Replacing the whole document on each keystroke loses concurrent work.
A transport protocol does not itself define a merge algorithm.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Choose a proven operational transformation or CRDT approach for the required semantics.
OT transforms operations against concurrent edits under its model.
CRDTs use identifiers and merge rules designed for convergence.
Both require careful implementation; do not invent a merge rule during the interview.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The client applies a local edit optimistically for responsiveness.
It sends an operation with the identifiers or base revision required by the algorithm.
The server persists and distributes accepted operations.
Clients integrate remote operations using the same defined algorithm.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d clarify offline requirements before choosing OT or a CRDT.”
“WebSockets carry edits; the concurrency algorithm defines how they merge.”
“I would use a mature implementation and explain its guarantees.”
“Convergence still needs a product decision about editing intent and conflict behavior.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does last-write-wins work for the whole document?
It converges by discarding one version, but can erase another user’s edits.
That may be acceptable for a simple settings field, not collaborative text.
A technically convergent result is not necessarily the user experience you want.

quiz.question: Why is whole-document last-write-wins a poor text-editing default?
options: It can discard concurrent user edits
quiz.explanation: Selecting one whole version loses changes present only in another concurrent version.

quiz.question: What does WebSocket transport provide here?
options: A communication channel, not merge semantics
quiz.explanation: Transport and collaborative data semantics are separate design concerns.

quiz.question: What should guide choosing OT versus a CRDT?
options: Required editing and offline semantics plus implementation constraints
quiz.explanation: Both are families of approaches with different coordination, metadata, and integration tradeoffs.

lessons.title: Collaborative docs: recover from a long disconnect
lessons.summary: Collaborative editor · Part 2 of 3: snapshots & operation logs.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A user reconnects after editing offline for an hour.
The document has also changed on other devices.
Replaying its entire lifetime history would be expensive.
You need a compact recovery base without losing merge information.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A text snapshot alone may omit metadata required by the merge algorithm.
Offline operations may reference elements or revisions absent from a naive snapshot.
The server must avoid applying repeated operations twice.
History compaction can make very old clients incompatible without a recovery policy.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Persist snapshots with the algorithm-specific state and a known log boundary.
Retain subsequent operations for catch-up.
Assign stable operation identities and deduplicate retries.
Define what happens when a client is older than the supported history horizon.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The reconnecting client reports its known revision or causal state.
The server sends missing operations or a compatible snapshot plus tail.
Pending local edits are integrated using the chosen algorithm’s protocol.
The client persists the resulting state before acknowledging durable local progress.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d use snapshots to bound replay cost, not to erase required metadata.”
“The snapshot and log boundary must form one coherent recovery point.”
“Old offline clients need an explicit resynchronization policy.”
“Repeated operation delivery should be harmless.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can every tombstone be deleted immediately after a character disappears?
Some algorithms need historical identifiers for later merges.
Safe garbage collection depends on causal knowledge and the offline-support contract.
Treat metadata retention as part of the algorithm, not an arbitrary TTL.

quiz.question: Why can a plain text snapshot be insufficient?
options: Merge algorithms may require identifiers or causal metadata
quiz.explanation: Visible content alone may not preserve the state required to merge future or delayed operations correctly.

quiz.question: What must accompany a snapshot for reliable replay?
quiz.explanation: The boundary determines which subsequent operations must still be applied.

quiz.question: Why not remove all merge tombstones immediately?
options: Late operations may still reference their identifiers
Deleted text must always remain visible
Every tombstone is an active user
quiz.explanation: Safe cleanup depends on the algorithm and the supported offline horizon.

lessons.title: Collaborative docs: separate presence from content
lessons.summary: Collaborative editor · Part 3 of 3: access & degraded operation.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A document has hundreds of viewers and several active editors.
Cursor updates are frequent, while text edits must be preserved.
An owner revokes one collaborator’s access during an open session.
The design needs different guarantees for presence, edits, and authorization.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Persisting every cursor movement wastes resources.
Dropping a text edit silently loses user work.
An open socket can outlive the permission decision that created it.
Cached permissions can leave a revoked editor temporarily able to submit work.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use ephemeral, rate-limited presence updates with expiration.
Keep accepted document operations on a durable path.
Authorize every edit under an appropriate current permission policy.
Invalidate sessions or check permission versions when access changes.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The gateway routes durable edits to the document’s collaboration owner.
Presence updates use a separate best-effort channel.
An access change updates authoritative membership and its version.
Stale sessions are rejected or refreshed before further edits are accepted.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d give presence and content different reliability budgets.”
“A missing cursor update is acceptable; a silently lost edit is not.”
“Authorization must remain valid after the socket is established.”
“For very large documents, I’d bound fan-out and isolate hot sessions.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what should an offline client do after its access is revoked?
Do not accept its edits merely because they were created earlier.
Offer a local export or recovery experience if the product permits it.
The server’s current access policy determines whether new synchronization is allowed.

quiz.question: Which traffic can usually be best-effort?
quiz.explanation: Presence can expire and refresh; content and permission state require stronger guarantees.

quiz.question: Does authenticating a socket once guarantee future edit authorization?
quiz.explanation: Long-lived sessions must still respect later access changes.

quiz.question: What should govern edits uploaded after access revocation?
options: Only the client’s old permission cache
quiz.explanation: Previously valid local access does not automatically authorize future server writes.

lessons.title: Web crawler: build a polite frontier
lessons.summary: Web crawler · Part 1 of 3: scheduling & scope.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design a crawler that collects public pages for a search index.
Clarify allowed domains, crawl purpose, freshness, and scale.
Assume permission-aware public crawling with a defined domain scope.
The frontier is the set of URLs waiting for controlled fetching.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A page can link to thousands of other pages or create an infinite URL space.
Unbounded fetching can overload both your workers and destination websites.
URL variants may refer to the same resource, but normalization can change meaning.
Politeness and scope are core requirements, not afterthoughts.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Maintain a durable frontier keyed by a carefully normalized URL.
Apply domain scope, robots policy, and per-host request budgets.
Track discovered, scheduled, fetched, and failed states.
Use bounded retries and cap crawl depth or patterns that create traps.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
Seed URLs enter the frontier under the crawl policy.
A host-aware scheduler releases eligible URLs to fetch workers.
Workers parse links and submit permitted discoveries back to the frontier.
Page content and fetch metadata go to durable storage for indexing.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d design the frontier and host budgets before increasing worker count.”
“The crawler must respect scope and destination load.”
“Normalization needs conservative rules because some URL parameters matter.”
“Discovered links reenter policy checks instead of bypassing them.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: is a robots policy enough to make any crawling acceptable?
No; access rules, terms, authentication boundaries, and rate considerations still matter.
Do not treat discovery as permission to access private resources.
Keep the exercise focused on authorized public content and explicit crawl limits.

quiz.question: Why schedule by host?
options: To control destination load and politeness
quiz.explanation: Host-level budgets prevent many workers from overwhelming one website at once.

quiz.question: Why can aggressive URL normalization be dangerous?
options: It may merge URLs with different meanings
quiz.explanation: Query parameters and path semantics may affect the represented resource.

quiz.question: What should newly discovered links do?
options: Pass through scope and scheduling policy
quiz.explanation: Discovery does not override the crawler’s access and workload constraints.

lessons.title: Web crawler: deduplicate without pretending certainty
lessons.summary: Web crawler · Part 2 of 3: frontier scale & content identity.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The crawler discovers billions of links with many repeats.
Keeping every membership check in one database becomes expensive.
The interviewer suggests a Bloom filter to reduce lookups.
Explain what it can and cannot prove.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A Bloom filter can report a false positive: “possibly seen” for a new URL.
