If every positive is dropped, some new pages will never be crawled.
URL deduplication and identical-content detection solve different problems.
Two URLs may have the same content, while one URL changes over time.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use a probabilistic filter only under an acceptable coverage policy.
For high recall, consult authoritative membership when the filter says possibly present.
Track fetch identity by normalized URL and content identity by a suitable hash.
Partition frontier ownership while keeping per-host scheduling coordinated.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A discovery first passes a fast membership filter.
Definite negatives proceed to an atomic authoritative insert.
Possible positives use the configured verification or skip policy.
Fetched content is hashed separately to avoid redundant indexing or storage.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would state the Bloom filter’s false-positive tradeoff.”
“It is not an exact visited-set replacement when complete coverage matters.”
“A unique insert still handles races between discoveries.”
“Content hashes help a different stage than URL scheduling.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does a content hash tell you when a page should be fetched again?
No; it identifies bytes or normalized content already retrieved.
Recrawl timing depends on change rate, importance, and freshness objectives.
The system cannot discover a changed page merely by remembering its old hash.

quiz.question: What can a Bloom filter positive mean?
options: The URL definitely exists in the exact set
The page is safe to publish
The URL may have been seen, but could be new
quiz.explanation: Standard Bloom filters allow false positives, so positive membership is not definitive.

quiz.question: What happens if every filter positive is skipped?
options: Some uncrawled URLs may be missed
quiz.explanation: False positives become missed discoveries unless another path verifies them.

quiz.question: What is different about content deduplication?
options: It compares fetched content rather than URL identity
quiz.explanation: Different URLs can yield the same content, and one URL can yield different content over time.

lessons.title: Web crawler: freshness under an adversarial web
lessons.summary: Web crawler · Part 3 of 3: recrawl & resource safety.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A few pages change every minute while most change rarely.
Some URLs redirect repeatedly or return enormous compressed responses.
A crawler has finite bandwidth, CPU, and storage.
Spend the budget on useful freshness while bounding hostile inputs.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A uniform recrawl interval wastes requests on stable pages.
Redirect loops and decompression bombs can consume worker resources.
User-provided seed URLs can also target internal network services.
A redirect can change the destination after the initial URL was checked.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Prioritize recrawls using observed change rate and content importance.
Use conditional requests where supported to avoid transferring unchanged bodies.
Enforce response size, decompression, duration, and redirect limits.
Restrict network destinations and revalidate every redirect and resolved target.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The scheduler assigns a next-fetch time based on freshness policy.
A worker validates the destination and fetches within resource bounds.
It records status, validators, content hash, and change observations.
Those observations adjust future scheduling; failures back off instead of hammering the host.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would optimize freshness per unit of crawl budget.”
“Conditional requests save bytes but still consume request capacity.”
“Every fetched document is untrusted input.”
“Destination validation must survive redirects and DNS changes.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should a frequently failing URL be retried more aggressively?
Usually not; bounded backoff protects both sides.
Distinguish transient failures from persistent exclusion or invalid content.
Keep failure history so the scheduler can make informed choices.

quiz.question: What guides adaptive recrawl frequency?
quiz.explanation: A freshness budget should focus effort where updates matter and are likely.

quiz.question: Why revalidate redirected destinations?
options: A redirect can lead to a forbidden or internal target
Redirects always preserve the original address
quiz.explanation: Initial validation does not cover a different destination introduced later in the request chain.

quiz.question: Why bound decompressed response size?
options: Small compressed input can expand into excessive resource use
quiz.explanation: Resource limits must apply to the representation actually processed, not only the transferred bytes.

lessons.title: Inference: define the serving contract
lessons.summary: ML inference platform · Part 1 of 3: latency & model lifecycle.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design an API that serves a trained machine-learning model.
Clarify input size, latency target, request rate, and model update frequency.
Assume interactive predictions with a stated deadline, plus a separate batch workload.
Treat these as workload assumptions, not guarantees every model can meet.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Model loading and preprocessing can dominate a small prediction’s latency.
Different model versions may produce different outputs for the same input.
Large requests can monopolize compute.
Returning a prediction without version context makes incidents hard to reproduce.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Keep model workers warm and separate loading from request admission.
Version the model, preprocessing pipeline, and relevant feature contract.
Validate inputs and enforce resource limits before expensive execution.
Return prediction metadata that permits tracing the served version.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The API validates input and resolves the active model version.
A bounded scheduler routes the request to a compatible warm worker.
The worker preprocesses, executes, and formats the result.
The response records latency and model identity without exposing private input data in logs.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would start from the latency and throughput targets, then measure model cost.”
“The serving version includes preprocessing, not just weight files.”
“Admission control protects finite model capacity.”
“Batch and interactive workloads should not compete without an explicit policy.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: should every prediction be cached?
Only when repeated inputs are semantically equivalent under the same version and context.
Include tenant and authorization boundaries where outputs depend on them.
Randomness, changing features, and sensitive inputs complicate cache validity.

quiz.question: Why version preprocessing alongside model weights?
options: It changes the effective input and output behavior
It only changes the website font
quiz.explanation: Different preprocessing can change predictions even with identical model weights.

quiz.question: What should happen before expensive inference?
quiz.explanation: Early bounds protect scarce resources and prevent invalid requests from consuming model capacity.

quiz.question: When is prediction caching appropriate?
options: Only when the model has no name
When request context and version make reuse valid
For every random or personalized output automatically
quiz.explanation: Cache correctness depends on all output-affecting inputs and access boundaries.

lessons.title: Inference: batch carefully, shed deliberately
lessons.summary: ML inference platform · Part 2 of 3: scheduling & capacity.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A GPU processes a batch more efficiently than individual requests.
The interviewer asks why you do not wait for the largest possible batch.
Interactive requests have deadlines, and demand fluctuates.
Throughput gains are useful only if user latency remains acceptable.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Batch formation adds queueing time before execution begins.
Large or long requests can block shorter ones.
Adding GPUs takes time if model loading is slow.
An unbounded queue turns overload into timeouts after wasted work.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use dynamic batching with maximum size and maximum wait time.
Separate incompatible shapes or workloads when the runtime requires it.
Bound queue depth and reject requests that cannot meet their budget.
Scale using queue age and measured utilization, accounting for worker warm-up.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The scheduler groups compatible requests within a short deadline-aware window.
A warm worker executes the selected batch.
Results are mapped back to individual request identities.
Expired or canceled work is removed when feasible before it consumes more compute.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d optimize useful throughput under a latency SLO.”
“Batch size and maximum wait are joint tuning parameters.”
“Queue age tells me whether users are waiting too long.”
“When capacity is exhausted, early rejection can be better than inevitable late failure.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: can you calculate latency from GPU utilization alone?
No; queueing, preprocessing, batching delay, and network work also contribute.
A highly utilized GPU can be efficient or badly overloaded.
Measure end-to-end latency and its components across realistic request mixes.

quiz.question: Why not wait indefinitely to fill a batch?
options: Bigger batches always reduce every user’s latency
Batch formation consumes the request’s latency budget
quiz.explanation: Throughput efficiency must be balanced against waiting time and deadlines.

quiz.question: What metric reveals waiting before GPU execution?
quiz.explanation: Queue age directly measures delay that hardware utilization alone can hide.

quiz.question: Why reject overload early?
options: To avoid spending resources on requests that will miss their budget
To eliminate all need for scaling
quiz.explanation: Bounded admission protects useful work and gives clients an honest response sooner.

lessons.title: Inference: release models without guessing
lessons.summary: ML inference platform · Part 3 of 3: evaluation & rollout.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
A new model looks better on an offline benchmark.
You want to release it without harming production users.
The interviewer asks how to compare versions and roll back.
Serving health and prediction quality need separate evaluation paths.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
A model can be accurate offline but slow or unstable in serving.
Live feature distributions may differ from training data.
Ground-truth labels may arrive days after the prediction.
A fast rollback of weights may fail if feature or schema compatibility changed.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Use versioned artifacts and a controlled routing layer.
Shadow selected requests where permitted, without exposing shadow outputs to users.
Canary a bounded traffic segment and monitor latency, errors, and quality proxies.
Retain compatible prior artifacts and feature contracts for a defined rollback window.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A release passes offline evaluation and compatibility gates.
Shadow or canary traffic gathers production evidence under access controls.
Routing expands only when explicit acceptance criteria are met.
If a gate fails, routing returns to a compatible known version and the incident is investigated.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d evaluate operational health and model quality independently.”
“Shadow results are observations, not user-visible decisions.”
“Delayed labels require later quality monitoring, not just launch-day metrics.”
“Rollback includes feature and preprocessing compatibility.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does distribution drift prove the model is wrong?
No; input changes are a signal to investigate, not direct proof of quality loss.
Where possible, compare against labeled outcomes and relevant slices.
Avoid treating a convenient proxy as the exact business objective.

quiz.question: What does shadow traffic mean in this design?
options: Evaluate a candidate without using its output for the user response
Give every user the new model immediately
quiz.explanation: Shadow execution gathers comparison evidence while the primary path still controls visible decisions.

quiz.question: Why can rollback need more than old weights?
options: Features and preprocessing contracts may have changed
Rollback always requires a new UI
quiz.explanation: The old model must receive compatible inputs and runtime behavior to reproduce its prior function.

quiz.question: Does detected input drift prove quality degradation?
options: Only if the chart is red
No; it is evidence to investigate
quiz.explanation: Drift and predictive quality are related but distinct; labeled outcomes give stronger quality evidence.

lessons.title: RAG: index documents with their permissions
lessons.summary: Retrieval-augmented assistant · Part 1 of 3: ingestion & retrieval.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Design an assistant that answers questions from company documents.
Clarify tenant isolation, citations, freshness, and unsupported-question behavior.
Assume private documents and a requirement to cite supporting passages.
The retrieval system must preserve access rules as well as text meaning.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
An embedding captures similarity, not whether a user may read the source.
Large chunks can mix topics; tiny chunks can lose context.
A document update can leave old chunks in the index.
Retrieved text may contain instructions that should not control the application.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Parse documents into versioned chunks with source and permission metadata.
Embed them using a recorded model version and maintain a retrieval index.
Apply access filtering during candidate retrieval and before exposing results.
Treat retrieved content as untrusted evidence, never as privileged instructions.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
An ingestion worker extracts content and chunk boundaries.
It records document version, chunk identity, source location, and access scope.
The query path retrieves only eligible candidate evidence.
The generator receives bounded passages and returns an answer with traceable citations.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would make permissions part of retrieval, not a UI filter afterward.”
“Each chunk keeps its source and document version.”
“Chunking balances local relevance against enough context to answer.”
“Retrieved instructions do not override the system’s tool or access policy.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: does vector similarity prove a passage supports an answer?
No; semantic resemblance can retrieve contradictory or irrelevant text.
Support must be assessed in generation and evaluation.
If evidence is insufficient, the assistant should say so rather than fabricate certainty.

quiz.question: Why attach permission metadata to chunks?
options: Retrieval must preserve document access boundaries
Citations remove the need for access checks
quiz.explanation: A useful semantic match can still be unauthorized for the requesting user.

quiz.question: Does a high similarity score prove factual support?
options: Only when the chunk is long
quiz.explanation: Similarity is a retrieval signal, not a logical guarantee that the passage supports the claim.

quiz.question: How should instructions found inside a retrieved document be treated?
options: As permission to access other tenants
As untrusted content, not application authority
As higher priority than system policy
quiz.explanation: Document text is evidence supplied to the assistant, not authority to change its operating rules.

lessons.title: RAG: improve retrieval before buying a bigger model
lessons.summary: Retrieval-augmented assistant · Part 2 of 3: quality & latency.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
The assistant gives fluent answers but cites the wrong pages.
The interviewer suggests switching to a larger generator.
That may increase cost without recovering missing evidence.
Diagnose the retrieval and generation stages separately.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Vector search can miss exact IDs, codes, or rare names.
Keyword search can miss paraphrases and conceptual matches.
Reranking every document is too expensive.
Long context can bury useful evidence and consume the latency budget.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Combine lexical and vector candidate retrieval when the workload benefits.
Use a bounded reranker to select stronger evidence from that pool.
Pack diverse, relevant passages within a controlled token budget.
Evaluate retrieval recall and citation support separately from answer fluency.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
The query produces lexical and semantic candidate sets.
Access-filtered results are merged and deduplicated by source identity.
A reranker scores a bounded shortlist.
The generator receives selected evidence with source identifiers it can cite.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I would inspect whether the right passage reached the model.”
“Hybrid retrieval addresses different kinds of matching failures.”
“Reranking spends compute on a shortlist, not the entire corpus.”
“A larger generator cannot reliably cite evidence that was never retrieved.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: which metric would you improve first?
Use a representative question set with known supporting passages.
Measure whether retrieval includes those passages before judging answer wording.
Then evaluate factual support, appropriate abstention, latency, and cost together.

quiz.question: Why use hybrid retrieval?
options: It guarantees every answer is correct
Exact terms and semantic matches have complementary strengths
quiz.explanation: Lexical and vector retrieval can recover different useful candidates for the same question.

quiz.question: Why inspect retrieval before upgrading the generator?
options: Larger models are always slower by definition
Missing evidence may be the actual bottleneck
quiz.explanation: If the supporting passage never enters context, better generation alone may not fix the citation failure.

quiz.question: What should a retrieval evaluation measure?
options: Whether known supporting passages appear in candidates
Only whether the answer sounds confident
Only the number of generated words
quiz.explanation: Retrieval recall isolates evidence discovery from later generation behavior.

lessons.title: RAG: defend your complete interview answer
lessons.summary: Retrieval-augmented assistant · Part 3 of 3: freshness & synthesis.

interview.context: Original interview-style practice. Workload numbers are illustrative assumptions, not claims about any company’s production architecture.

cards.title: The interviewer asks…
cards.label: Interview prompt
cards.body:
Finish by presenting an end-to-end private-document assistant design.
The interviewer asks about updates, deletion, latency, and failure recovery.
Use the same structure you can reuse for any system-design question.
Start with requirements, then defend the critical path and tradeoffs.

cards.title: Find the hard part
cards.label: The challenge
cards.body:
Deleted documents can remain in vector indexes, caches, and generated-answer caches.
A permission change may invalidate a previously safe cached answer.
Model or embedding upgrades can break compatibility with old representations.
One “RAG quality” score hides several different failure modes.

cards.title: Make a clear design choice
cards.label: Design decision
cards.body:
Track document and index generations and process updates through a durable pipeline.
Use tombstones and current authorization checks to block stale evidence exposure.
Key any answer cache by the relevant version and authorization context.
Release embedding changes through a compatible reindex-and-switch process.

cards.title: Walk through the system
cards.label: Request walkthrough
cards.body:
A user query is authenticated and bounded by a latency budget.
Eligible evidence is retrieved, reranked, and checked against current source state.
Generation produces supported citations or an explicit insufficient-evidence response.
Tracing records stage timings and source versions without leaking private documents.

cards.title: Say it in the interview
cards.label: Your spoken answer
cards.body:
“I’d clarify the user promise, scope, scale, and strongest invariant first.”
“Then I’d walk one request and explain each component’s responsibility.”
“I’d quantify the bottleneck and name the failure-recovery path.”
“Finally, I’d state what is approximate, what is guaranteed, and what I would measure.”

cards.title: Handle the follow-up
cards.label: Interviewer follow-up
cards.body:
Follow-up: what is the best architecture in an interview?
One whose choices follow from the stated requirements and workload.
Explain the baseline before adding complexity, and revisit assumptions openly.
A defensible tradeoff is stronger than a diagram filled with fashionable tools.

quiz.question: Why can a cached answer become unsafe after a permission change?
options: Model weights automatically revoke every answer
It may contain evidence the user can no longer access
Cached text never includes source information
quiz.explanation: Answer caching must respect current access policy and relevant source/version context.

quiz.question: Why can changing embedding models require reindexing?
options: Old and new vector spaces may be incompatible
Every embedding has the same semantics
Reindexing is only a visual operation
quiz.explanation: Query and document representations must be compatible for meaningful similarity retrieval.

quiz.question: What makes a system-design answer convincing?
options: The greatest possible number of services
Claiming zero latency and no failures
Requirements-linked choices with explicit tradeoffs and recovery
quiz.explanation: A strong answer connects scope, workload, invariants, architecture, and operational behavior coherently.
